q: This man originally served under Liu Zhang but later became one of Liu Bei's key advisers. He helped plan the seizure of Yi Province and accompanied Liu Bei in the contest for Hanzhong. He died of illness before Liu Bei did, and so had no part in the deathbed entrustment. Who was he?
reply:
The man is **Fa Zheng** (法正, courtesy name Fa Xiaozhi). The records support each part of your description, and he died before Liu Bei.

He first served Liu Zhang. 「正與同郡孟達俱入蜀依劉璋，久之為新都令，後召署軍議校尉」 ("Fa Zheng and Meng Da, both from the same commandery, entered Shu to serve Liu Zhang. After a long time he became Magistrate of Xindu, and was later summoned to serve as Military Discussion Colonel.") [2]. When Liu Zhang asked whom to send as envoy to Liu Bei, 「松乃舉正」 ("Zhang Song then recommended Zheng") [2]. Fa Zheng then secretly offered Liu Bei a strategy: 「正既宣旨，陰獻策於先主」 ("After delivering his message, he secretly offered a plan to the Former Ruler") [2]. Liu Zhang then 「遣法正請先主」 ("sent Fa Zheng to invite the Former Ruler") [4]. After Liu Bei besieged Chengdu, 「璋出降」 ("Liu Zhang came out and surrendered") [3]. Afterwards, Liu Bei's arrangement of his men named Fa Zheng as 「法正為謀主」 ("Fa Zheng as chief strategist") [3].

For Hanzhong, the text records that 「先主善其策，乃率諸將進兵漢中，正亦從行」 ("The Former Ruler approved his plan, led the generals to advance on Hanzhong, and Zheng accompanied him") [7]. At Dingjun and Xingshi, Fa Zheng said 「可擊矣」 ("We can attack") and Huang Zhong's assault 「大破淵軍」 ("greatly defeated Xiahou Yuan's army") [7].

His death is recorded after Liu Bei became King of Hanzhong. 「先主立為漢中王，以正為尚書令、護軍將軍。明年卒，時年四十五」 ("When the Former Ruler became King of Hanzhong, he appointed Zheng as Shangshu Ling and Hujun Jiangjun. He died the following year, aged forty-five") [1]. The Hanzhong title was granted in 建安二十四年 [13], so by the text's wording Fa Zheng died in 建安二十五年. I have not converted this to a Western year. 「先主為之流涕者累日」 ("The Former Ruler wept for him for several days") [1].

I did not retrieve the passage describing Liu Bei's deathbed entrustment, so I cannot quote it. The later remark by Zhuge Liang, 「法孝直若在，則能制主上」 ("If Fa Xiaozhi were alive, he could have restrained the ruler") [1], which refers to the 章武二年 defeat, indicates that Fa Zheng was no longer alive by then. From his death in 建安二十五年 and that remark, it can be inferred that he could not have had any role in Liu Bei's final arrangements.

q: One side had the advantage in troops and supplies; the other, in a prolonged standoff, was running short of grain. In the end the weaker side, acting on intelligence from a defector, raided the enemy's main grain depot and turned the battle around. Which battle was this, and who was the defector?
reply:
The battle was **Guandu (官渡)**, fought between Cao Cao and Yuan Shao in 建安五年 (the fifth year of the Jian'an era), according to 《荀彧传》[4]. The defector was **Xu You (许攸, styled Ziyuan 子远)**, once an adviser to Yuan Shao [1][6]. I did not convert the year to a Common Era date.

**The standoff and grain shortage.** Cao Cao held Guandu while Yuan Shao surrounded him, and 「太祖軍糧方盡」[4] ("Cao's army was about to run out of grain"). They had been in contact for months: 「公與紹相拒連月」[6] ("Gong and Shao faced each other for several months"). Cao Cao also told the grain carriers 「却十五日爲汝破紹」[6] ("in fifteen days I will defeat Yuan Shao for you"). Yuan's side had the larger supply train: 「袁紹運穀車數千乘至」[6] ("Yuan Shao's grain carts, several thousand, arrived").

**The defection.** The sources give two reasons. In 《魏略》, Xu You 「知不可爲謀，乃亡詣太祖」[1] ("knew he could not make a plan for Yuan, and so fled to Cao Cao"), after Yuan had refused his advice not to fight Cao [1]. In 《荀彧传》, Yuan's official Shen Pei 「以許攸家不法，收其妻子，攸怒叛紹」[4] ("arrested Xu You's wife and children for his family's misconduct, and Xu You, angry, rebelled against Yuan"). These accounts differ and I cannot reconcile them from the sources.

**The raid.** Xu You told Cao Cao that Yuan's supplies were at 「故市、烏巢，屯軍無嚴備」[2] ("Gushi and Wuchao, where the garrison had no strict defenses") and advised a light raid to 「燔其積聚」[2] ("burn their stores"). Cao Cao's aides doubted the plan, but 荀攸 and 賈詡 urged him to go ahead [6]. Cao Cao left 曹洪 to hold the camp and led 五千 men by night, 「皆用袁軍旗幟」[2] ("all carrying Yuan's banners") [6]. They 「盡燔其糧穀寶貨」[2] ("burned all the grain and treasure"), and 淳于瓊 and the other commanders were killed [4][6]. Afterward 「紹衆大潰，紹及譚棄軍走，渡河」[6] ("Yuan's army collapsed, and Yuan and his son Tan abandoned their army and fled across the river").

**A dispute about numbers.** Pei Songzhi (裴松之) disputed the common picture of Cao Cao as badly outnumbered. He wrote 「是不得甚少」[14] ("Cao's force could not have been very small"), giving several reasons. This is Pei's own argument, not a record of fact, and the sources do not settle the question.

q: A strategic proposal called for first occupying Jing and Yi Provinces, allying with Sun Quan, waiting for a change in the situation in the north, and then advancing along two routes. If Jing Province were lost, which key precondition of this strategy would no longer hold?
reply:
The strategy is Zhuge Liang's proposal to Liu Bei, the Longzhong Plan. Losing Jing Province would break the plan's requirement to hold both Jing and Yi, and it would also end the alliance with Sun Quan.

The proposal states: 「若跨有荊、益，保其巖阻，西和諸戎，南撫夷越，外結好孫權，內修政理」 ("If you hold both Jing and Yi, secure their strongholds, make peace with the western tribes, pacify the southern peoples, form good relations with Sun Quan, and set right governance internally") [2]. It then says that when the world changes, 「則命一上將將荊州之軍以向宛、洛，將軍身率益州之眾出於秦川」 ("one senior general leads the Jing army toward Wan and Luo, and you personally lead the Yi army out through Qinchuan") [2]. Jing is the base for the eastern route and Yi for the western one.

Losing Jing removes the base for the eastern route. The alliance also failed in the same province. After Guan Yu drove out the officials Sun Quan had installed in the southern commanderies, Sun Quan 「權大怒，乃遣呂蒙督鮮於丹、徐忠、孫規等兵二萬取長沙、零陵、桂陽三郡」 [17]. Lü Meng then took the Jing territory, and 「權使朱然、潘璋斷其徑路，即父子俱獲，荊州遂定」 [20]. Guan Yu and his son Guan Ping were executed at Linju [27]. The two states had earlier divided Jing between them, with the east going to Sun Quan [17].

Later, Liu Bei fought Wu and was defeated at Yiling [35]. Lu Xun had warned that 「夷陵要害，國之關限，雖為易得，亦復易失。失之非徒損一郡之地，荊州可憂」 ("Yiling is a key pass of the state, easy to take and easy to lose. Losing it would not only cost one commandery; Jing would be in danger") [31]. The sources do not state Liu Bei's aim in that campaign.

Inference: without Jing, the eastern arm of the plan has no base to launch from, and the alliance that was meant to secure the flank broke over the same province. The records show the alliance renewed later. Zhuge Liang sent envoys to Wu and 「因結和親，遂為與國」 [1], and 「與權連和」 [5]. But the original two-front plan could no longer rest on Jing.

q: Cao Cao took in Emperor Xian of Han and issued orders in the name of the Han central government. Compared with relying on military strength alone, what political advantage did this chiefly bring him?
reply:
**Short answer:** The records suggest the main advantage was political legitimacy. Holding the emperor let Cao Cao act in the dynasty's name, cast rival warlords as opponents of the court, and attract people who would not follow him otherwise. The sources give these as the arguments of Cao's advisers and rivals, not as measured results.

**Acting for the dynasty.** When Xun Yu urged Cao Cao to bring the court to Xu, he argued that serving the emperor would follow the people's wishes and attract heroes and talent: 「奉主上以從民望，大順也；秉至公以服雄傑，大略也；扶弘義以致英俊，大德也」[2]. Mao Jie gave similar advice: 「宜奉天子以令不臣」[17]. The emperor then granted Cao his titles: 「天子拜太祖大將軍」[2] and 「天子拜公司空」[18].

**Issuing orders in the emperor's name.** Cao Cao could claim the emperor's authority for his campaigns. In one case, Lü Bu was persuaded by an imperial edict, 「并詔書購捕公孫瓚、袁術、韓暹、楊奉等」[30]. Rivals also recognized the value of the emperor's name. Yuan Shao was angry that Cao 「挾天子以令我」[1]. Tian Feng had urged Yuan Shao to strike Xu early, arguing that 「若挾天子以令諸侯，四海可指麾而定」[5]. Shen Shou advised Yuan Shao to bring the emperor to Ye and 「挾天子而令諸侯」[7]. The phrase suggests the emperor's name was seen as a source of authority over other warlords.

**Attracting defectors.** Jia Xu's advice to Zhang Xiu gives the clearest reasons for joining Cao: 「夫曹公奉天子以令天下，其宜從一也」[13]. He added that Cao was weaker and would be glad to have them, and that a man with ambitions for supremacy would put aside private grudges [13]. Zhang Xiu then 「率衆歸太祖」[13].

**Limits of the evidence.** The sources do not show how much the emperor's authority changed the outcome of any given campaign. The advantage was also disputed. Guo Tu argued that bringing the emperor close would limit Yuan Shao's power: 「從之則權輕，違之則拒命」[7]. He held that the prize went to 「先得者王」[7]. Pei Songzhi noted that the text attributes Guo Tu's plan differently from the main biography of Yuan Shao, and he judged that the main biography is the more reliable account [7]. Xun Yu also opposed raising Cao's rank, because Cao 「本興義兵以匡朝寧國」[20] and should not seek more honors.

q: This man first served Yüan Shao and later went over to Ts'ao Ts'ao. He fought in Han-chung, defeated Ma Su at Chieh-t'ing, and finally died at Mu-men while pursuing the Shu army. Who was he?
reply:
**Answer: Zhang He (張郃, styled Junyi 雋乂), a general of Wei.**

**Service under Yuan Shao and defection to Cao Cao.** Zhang He first served Han Fu and then led his troops over to Yuan Shao. After Yuan Shao's camp was defeated at Wuchao, Guo Tu slandered him, and 「郃懼，乃歸太祖。」[1] (Zhang He, afraid, went over to Cao Cao.) Cao Cao received him, and 「拜郃偏將軍，封都亭侯。」[10] (He was appointed Colonel-Conqueror and enfeoffed as Marquis of Duting.)

**Hanzhong.** After Cao Cao defeated Zhang Lu, 「太祖還，留郃與夏侯淵等守漢中，拒劉備。」[10] (Cao Cao left Zhang He with Xiahou Yuan and others to hold Hanzhong against Liu Bei.) Zhang He was later checked by Zhang Fei at Dangqu (宕渠), 「爲備將張飛所拒，引還南鄭」[10] (and withdrew to Nanzheng). After Xiahou Yuan was killed, his subordinate Guo Huai urged the troops to follow Zhang He, saying 「張將軍，國家名將，劉備所憚」[11] (General Zhang is the state's famous general, feared by Liu Bei), and the army then placed itself under his command.

**Jieting (街亭).** 「魏明帝西鎮長安，命張郃拒亮，亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破。」[13] (Ma Su disobeyed Zhuge Liang's orders and was badly defeated by Zhang He.) The Wei biography adds that 「郃絶其汲道，擊，大破之。」[16] (Zhang He cut off Ma Su's water supply and attacked, defeating him badly.)

**Death at Mumen (木門).** Chen Shou's biography says: 「諸葛亮復出祁山，詔郃督諸將西至略陽，亮還保祁山，郃追至木門，與亮軍交戰，飛矢中郃右膝，薨」[17] (When Zhuge Liang came out again at Qishan and then withdrew to hold Qishan, Zhang He pursued him to Mumen, where an arrow struck his right knee and he died.)

The sources differ on how he died and where:
- Pei Songzhi's annotation quotes the 《魏略》, which says Sima Yi ordered the pursuit against Zhang He's objection, and that the Shu army ambushed him: 「蜀軍乘高布伏，弓弩亂發，矢中郃髀。」[18] (The Shu troops set an ambush on high ground, crossbows fired wildly, and an arrow hit his thigh.)
- Chen Shou's biography of Liu Shan gives a different place: 「郃追至青封，與亮交戰，被箭死。」[20] (Zhang He pursued to Qingfeng, fought Zhuge Liang, and was killed by an arrow.)

So the main biography and the Liu Shan annals agree that he was killed by an arrow while pursuing Zhuge Liang, but they name different places (Mumen and Qingfeng). The record does not settle which is correct. The question's "Mu-men" follows Chen Shou's biography of Zhang He.

q: This man did not personally lead the army that conquered Shu, yet he pushed the war of conquest forward while he controlled the Cao-Wei court. His son later replaced Cao-Wei and founded the Western Jin. Who was he?
reply:
**Answer: Sima Zhao (司马昭, posthumously 晋文王), the younger brother of Sima Shi.** His son Sima Yan (司马炎) was his heir and later became the Jin emperor. The records I retrieved do not describe how the Western Jin was founded, so I can only speak to Sima Zhao's role and his son's position under him.

**Shu campaign.** Sima Zhao did not lead the army himself. The Han-Jin Chunqiu (《汉晋春秋》) quotes his letter to Sun Hao: 「故分命偏師，平定蜀漢，役未經年，全軍獨克」[11] (so he sent a detachment to pacify Shu-Han, and the campaign was won by one army in less than a year). The main text of Zhong Hui's biography says the army Zhong Hui led was 「五六倍於鄧艾」[6] (five or six times the size of Deng Ai's). When Zhong Hui reported that Deng Ai was disloyal, Sima Zhao 「將西」[6] (was about to go west). By the time he reached Chang'an, 「會果已死」[6] (Zhong Hui had already died). Sima Zhao was therefore not the field commander, and his role was to direct the war from the capital.

**Control of the court.** In 景元元年 he was promoted to 相國 (Chancellor), enfeoffed as 晉公, and given the Nine Bestowals (加九錫之禮)[4]. The Han-Jin Chunqiu records Emperor Gaogui (曹髦) saying 「司馬昭之心，路人所知也」[3] (Sima Zhao's intentions are known to every passerby). The emperor said this shortly before he was killed in the coup. The remark shows that Sima Zhao's ambitions were widely understood at the time. Whether that was the cause of anything else is not stated in the records.

**The son.** Sima Zhao named Sima Yan 世子 (heir) 「丙午，命撫軍大將軍新昌鄉侯炎為晉世子」[14], and made him deputy to the Chancellor 「命中撫軍司馬炎副貳相國事」[7]. After Sima Zhao died, 「晉太子炎紹封襲位，總攝百揆」[1] (Crown Prince Yan succeeded to the title and took over the administration of all offices). A later passage in the Wei Shizu (《魏世譜》) records 「晉受禪」[19] (the Jin accession by abdication), and a commentary notes that Sima Yan's mother's family line produced 「晉武帝」[18] (Emperor Wu of Jin), but the retrieved text does not narrate the transfer of the throne itself.

q: While Kuan Yü was attacking Fan in the north, Sun Ch'üan's side seized Chiang-ling and other places in his rear. Why could Kuan Yü still collapse so quickly overall, even though he had won a major victory on the northern front?
reply:
**Short answer:** The northern victory was narrower than it first looks. Guan Yu's army was undone less by the flooding at Fancheng than by a thin rear garrison, officers who resented him, and Lü Meng's surprise attack. Once Jingzhou fell, his soldiers had little reason to stay with him.

**The northern front was not a clean win.** In 建安二十四年, Guan Yu's forces captured Yu Jin and his seven armies after the flood, and Yu Jin surrendered: 「禁降羽」 [5]. But Cao Ren held Fancheng with a few thousand men, and the text says that when Xu Huang attacked from outside, Cao Ren broke out and 「羽退走」 [1]. The source also says that Guan Yu 「不能克」 Xu Huang's relief force [5]. Cao Cao's advisers proposed letting Sun Quan attack Guan Yu's rear and offering him southern territory, so that the siege would end: 「可遣人勸躡其後，許割江南以封權，則樊圍自解」 [4][5]. Cao Cao adopted this plan.

**The rear collapsed for several reasons:**

- **Thin garrisons.** Lü Meng argued that Guan Yu had left many troops to guard Gong'an and Nanjun because he feared an attack from behind: 「羽討樊而多留備兵，必恐蒙圖其後故也」. He predicted that if Lü Meng pretended to be sick, Guan Yu would 「必撤備兵，盡赴襄陽」 [9]. Guan Yu did pull back: 「羽果信之，稍撤兵以赴樊」 [9]. Sun Quan then sent Lü Meng forward [9][13].
- **Officers who resented him.** Earlier, Guan Yu had insulted Sun Quan's envoy over a marriage proposal, and Sun Quan was enraged [5]. Mi Fang and Shi Ren, who controlled the rear, 「素皆嫌羽輕己」 and did not fully supply him during the campaign, so Guan Yu said he would punish them later [5]. They grew afraid and secretly went over to Sun Quan [5]. Yang Xi's account says Shi Ren 「與羽有隙，叛迎孫權」 [17].
- **Surprise and the loss of families.** Lü Meng hid his best troops in boats and had men dressed as merchants and rowers, so that 「是故羽不聞知」 [9]. He then took Guan Yu's forces' families and treated them well [9]. Guan Yu's soldiers heard from home that their families were safe and were treated better than before, 「故羽吏士無鬬心」 [20]. Sun Quan 「盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」 [5].
- **Final collapse.** Guan Yu retreated toward Maicheng, and 「兵皆解散，尚十餘騎」 [13]. He himself 「自知孤窮」 [20]. The sources differ on the end. Guan Yu's own biography says he was killed at Linju (臨沮) [5]. Sun Quan's biography says Ma Zhong captured him at Zhangxiang (章鄉) [13]. Lü Meng's biography describes his retreat west to Zhangxiang, where the people abandoned him, and then the capture of him and his son [20].

**Chen Shou's judgment** points to the deeper cause: 「羽剛而自矜，飛暴而無恩，以短取敗，理數之常也」 [27]. Chen Shou ties Guan Yu's defeat to his own pride and his poor treatment of others.

**My inference:** The records show that Guan Yu's northern success did not protect his base. He left the rear lightly defended, and the officers who controlled it resented him and were willing to turn to Sun Quan. Lü Meng's deception then worked, and the loss of Jingzhou led to the collapse of his army. The sources do not say that Guan Yu meant to abandon Jingzhou, so this explanation rests on the order of events in the records, not on any direct statement of intent.

q: The Oath of the Peach Garden: after Liu Pei, Kuan Yü and Chang Fei swore brotherhood, what was the order of seniority among the three?
reply:
The sources I found do not give a full seniority order for the three. They show that Guan Yu was older than Zhang Fei, but they do not state Liu Bei's age or describe any oath.

- **Guan Yu and Zhang Fei:** Zhang Fei's biography says, "「羽年長數歲，飛兄事之」" [2]. Guan Yu was several years older, and Zhang Fei treated him as an elder brother.
- **Liu Bei:** Guan Yu's biography says, "「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟」" [1]. This describes a brotherly bond, but it gives no birth order. Liu Bei is called 先主 (the lord they served) throughout these passages, not by age.
- **The oath:** None of the passages I retrieved describes a Peach Garden oath. The version where Liu Bei is eldest, Guan Yu second and Zhang Fei youngest is the one in the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*. I have not checked that order against the *Sanguozhi* text, so I cannot confirm it from these sources.

q: Before the Battle of Red Cliffs, Liu Bei was comparatively weak, while Sun Quan held the Jiangdong territory and a navy. Given this imbalance, why did Sun Quan still have an incentive to ally with Liu Bei rather than stand by and let Cao Cao destroy him?
reply:
**Short answer:** The sources suggest Sun Quan was choosing between submitting to Cao Cao and fighting with a partner. Those urging surrender argued that submission would cost Sun his position. Sun himself said that only Liu Bei could resist Cao. The naval imbalance you describe was also narrower than it first looks.

**The surrender option.** After Cao Cao took Jingzhou, Sun's advisers pressed for submission. Cao's letter claimed 800,000 troops on land and water [9]. Zhou Yu countered that Cao's northern troops numbered only 「不過十五六萬」 (no more than 150,000 to 160,000), and that the men from Liu Biao's former forces were 「亦極七八萬耳」 (at most 70,000 to 80,000) [9]. Sun struck his table with his sword and warned that anyone who spoke of welcoming Cao would share its fate: 「諸將吏敢復有言當迎操者，與此案同」 [9]. Lu Su's argument shows the personal stakes. He said he could submit and keep a minor post, but Sun could not: 「今肅迎操，操當以肅還付鄉黨」 and 「將軍迎操，欲安所歸」 [14]. Lu Su's remarks are his own argument, but they show what Sun risked by surrendering.

**Why Liu Bei was the partner.** Sun said plainly that 「非劉豫州莫可以當曹操者」 [4]. This came in the debate with Zhuge Liang, who had argued that Sun should either ally with Liu Bei or submit [4]. Earlier, when Liu Biao died, Lu Su had advised Sun to work with Liu Bei, noting that Liu Bei 「與操有隙」 (had a grudge against Cao) [18]. Lu Fan later wanted to detain Liu Bei, but Lu Su opposed him, saying 「多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也」 [15], which the Han-Jin Chunqiu records. In this view, creating more enemies for Cao while building one's own support was the best plan. Cheng Yu, a Wei adviser, predicted the same logic from the other side: 「權必資之以禦我」 (Sun would have to rely on Liu Bei to resist us) [6].

**Why the naval edge did not decide it.** Zhou Yu's case for fighting rested on Cao's weaknesses. Cao's army was exhausted, and northerners were unused to water warfare [25]. Zhuge Liang made the same points, adding that Jingzhou's people had submitted only 「逼兵勢耳，非心服也」 (under military pressure, not from conviction) [11]. The surrender advocates also argued that Cao now held Liu Biao's navy, which had 「蒙沖鬥艦，乃以千數」 (thousands of assault and fighting ships), and that the Yangtze barrier was now shared: 「此為長江之險，已與我共之矣」 [31]. Liu Bei also had men. Zhuge Liang said that Liu Bei's returning troops and Guan Yu's navy numbered 「萬人」 (10,000), and that Liu Qi's men were no fewer than 10,000 more [4].

**How the alliance was made.** Sun answered Zhuge Liang with 「吾計決矣」 (my plan is set) [4]. He then sent Zhou Yu, Cheng Pu and Lu Su with 「水軍三萬」 (30,000 navy men) to join Liu Bei [11].

**Disputed credit.** Pei Songzhi argued that the anti-Cao plan was Lu Su's original idea, and that the Shu record crediting Zhuge Liang conflicts with the Wu account: 「而舛互若此」 [1]. In another note, Pei Songzhi says that Lu Su first proposed resistance, and that Zhou Yu 「但與肅闇同」 (only agreed with Lu Su in secret) [9]. Sun Sheng disputed the Jiuzhou Chunqiu story that Lu Su spoke for resistance only after Sun wanted to kill him, saying it was 「非其論也」 (not a sound account), since many had urged submission [12].

**Chen Shou's assessment.** Chen Shou credits Sun with 「屈身忍辱，任才尚計」 (enduring humiliation and valuing talent and strategy), and with being able to 「自擅江表，成鼎峙之業」 (rule the Jiangdong region on his own and establish a tripartite balance) [35]. He does not discuss the alliance decision itself.

**My inference.** The records suggest Sun's decision to ally was driven by three things. First, Sun believed he could not beat Cao alone, since he said 「吾不能舉全吳之地，十萬之眾，受制於人」 (I cannot give up all of Wu and its hundred thousand men to be controlled by another) [4]. Second, he saw submission as costing him his independence. Third, he judged Liu Bei the only partner who both opposed Cao and had men and a base to fight with. This is my inference from the arguments and the numbers cited, not something any source states outright.

q: A Cao-Wei emperor left Luoyang to pay respects at the imperial tombs, and a senior minister who had long pleaded illness seized the chance to take control of the capital and force the other regent to surrender his power. What event was this, and who set it in motion?
reply:
**Answer:** This was the Gaoping Tombs Incident (高平陵之变) of 249 (正始10年 by the era tables). Sima Yi, the Grand Tutor (太傅), set it in motion and took control of the capital from Cao Shuang, the other regent.

**What happened.** The emperor's carriage went to the Gaoping Tomb, and Cao Shuang and his brothers went with it. Sima Yi then "部勒兵馬，先據武庫，遂出屯洛水浮橋" (deployed his troops, first seized the arsenal, then camped at the Luo River pontoon bridge) [2]. He memorialized against Cao Shuang, accusing him of "內則僭擬，外專威權" (presuming to equal the ruler inside and monopolizing power outside) [2]. The Empress Dowager issued an edict ordering that his memorial be carried out: "皇太后令勑臣如奏施行" [2]. Cao Shuang and his brothers were dismissed and sent home as marquises [1][6].

**Who set it in motion.** Sima Yi did, and his feigned illness was the preparation. Cao Shuang's associates had urged him not to let Sima Yi share in government affairs, and "宣王遂稱疾避爽" (Sima Yi then pretended to be ill to avoid Cao Shuang) [5]. When Li Sheng visited him, Sima Yi "稱疾困篤，示以羸形" (pretended to be gravely ill and showed a frail appearance), and "勝不能覺，謂之信然" (Li Sheng did not notice and believed it) [2]. The Weishu comments that Sima Yi had earlier "力不能爭，且懼其禍，故避之" (been unable to compete and feared disaster, so he withdrew) [7].

**The surrender.** The sources differ on the details. The 《世語》 says Sima Yi sent Xu Yun and Chen Tai to persuade Cao Shuang, and that Yin Damu, a Palace Guards officer trusted by Cao Shuang, told him that he would "唯免官而已，以洛水爲誓" (only be dismissed, with an oath sworn on the Luo River) [14]. Cao Shuang believed this and withdrew his troops [14]. The same work records that Jiang Ji had written to Cao Shuang conveying Sima Yi's words that he would "惟免官而已", and that Cao Shuang was then executed; Jiang Ji regretted the broken promise and died of illness [17]. By contrast, another passage has Cao Shuang sending Xu Yun and Chen Tai to Sima Yi to confess and ask for death, after which Sima Yi's memorial was delivered [6]. The two accounts disagree about who sent the envoys, and I have not resolved which is right.

After Cao Shuang's dismissal, the 《魏末傳》 says Sima Yi had 800 men surround his residence [9]. The court later decided that Cao Shuang and his associates had plotted treason and ordered the extermination of their three clans [21].

q: Identify the person: when Cao Cao was routed at Wancheng, who held the camp gate and fought to the death to cover Cao Cao's retreat?
reply:
The man was **Dian Wei** (典韋). Cao Cao's own biography doesn't name him here. The account comes from Dian Wei's biography in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*.

When Zhang Xiu attacked Cao Cao's camp at Wancheng, Cao Cao sortied, lost, and withdrew with light cavalry: 「太祖出戰不利，輕騎引去」[3] ("The Taizu's sortie went badly, and he withdrew with light cavalry"). Dian Wei held the gate: 「韋戰於門中，賊不得入」[3] ("Wei fought in the gateway, and the enemy could not get in"). When his men scattered and the enemy poured in through other gates, he kept fighting. He took dozens of wounds, at one point clamping two attackers and beating them to death: 「韋雙挾兩賊擊殺之」[3]. He finally died glaring and cursing: 「瞋目大罵而死」[3].

Cao Cao wept when he heard of Dian Wei's death, had the body retrieved, and had him buried. He also made Dian Wei's son Dian Man a gentleman of the palace, and later a 都尉 (commandant) [3].

The Basic Annals of Emperor Wu confirm the setback: Cao Cao was hit by a stray arrow, and his eldest son Cao Ang (昂) and his nephew Cao Anmin (安民) were killed [13]. He then withdrew to Wuyin (舞陰) [13].

q: Shu-Han's main base was Yi Province, and its northern expeditions had to haul grain across the mountains to the front. Why did 'winning a battle at the front' not necessarily mean 'being able to hold the newly gained territory for long'?
reply:
**Short answer:** Shu could win battles at the front, but the grain came over the mountain roads from Shu and Hanzhong. In several recorded cases, running out of grain forced withdrawal. The territory taken also had no secure local base. The records show Shu's advances and withdrawals, but they do not state a single cause for failing to hold ground. The link between the two is my inference from the points below.

**Supply limited how long the army could stay**

- In Zhuge Liang's ninth year of Jianxing he "以木牛運，糧盡退軍" (used wooden oxen to carry grain, and withdrew when the grain ran out) [12]. In a winter campaign against Chencang, "糧盡而還" (his grain ran out and he turned back) [6].
- Zhang He read the situation this way: "亮縣軍無穀，不能久攻" (Zhuge Liang's army was cut off from grain and could not attack for long) [10].
- Zhuge Liang built transport tools to address this, "以流馬運" (transport by the "flowing horse") [17]. He also gathered grain at Xiegu Pass and built depots there [17]. A chapter of his collected writings is titled Chuanyun (傳運, on transport) [42].
- His biography states the problem directly: "亮每患糧不繼，使己志不申，是以分兵屯田，為久駐之基" (Zhuge Liang was always troubled that grain could not keep up, which kept his aims from being realized, so he split the army to farm and laid a base for a long stay) [12]. He died before that plan could show results [12].
- Wei's court also expected this. Some officials argued that "亮軍無輜重，糧必不繼" (Zhuge Liang's army had no baggage train, so its grain would surely run short) [8].
- Wei had its own supply problem in Longyou. In the fifth year of Taihe, "隴右無穀，議欲關中大運" (Longyou had no grain, so there was talk of a large transport from Guanzhong). Guo Huai instead won over the Qiang and Hu peoples so that households provided grain, and the army's food was sufficient [1].

**The conquered ground did not stay with Shu**

- In the sixth year of Jianxing, "南安、天水、安定三郡反應亮" (Nan'an, Tianshui and Anding rebelled to answer Zhuge Liang) [13]. Wei forces then pacified them, and the record says "三郡皆平" (all three were pacified) [13]. Zhang He also "破平之" (defeated and pacified them) [10].
- A Wei account gives the reason the three rebelled so readily: Wei had been quiet for years, so it was unprepared, and "故三郡同時應亮" (so the three commanderies answered Zhuge Liang together) [19].
- The commentary quoted from 《袁子》 in Pei Songzhi's annotation asks why Zhuge Liang did not press faster to take advantage of the rebellions. Its answer: "蜀兵輕銳，良將少，亮始出，未知中國彊弱" (Shu's soldiers were light and quick, its good generals were few, and when Zhuge Liang first marched out he did not know the strength of the Central Plains) [11]. This is one commentator's view, not a recorded event.
- Shu also could not depend on local grain. Wei's Shangyong wheat was the target: the Wei emperor refused to have it cut down, and "賴得此麥以爲軍糧" (they relied on that wheat for army grain) [8]. Zhuge Liang did cut the wheat himself: "因大芟刈其麥" [21]. Shu's food therefore depended on what it could seize from the enemy.
- Holding new ground would also have meant garrisoning it. Zhuge Liang's own reasoning about the southern territories (南中) states: "若留外人，則當留兵，兵留則無所食" (if he left outsiders in charge, he would have to leave troops there, and troops left behind would have no food) [16]. That passage concerns the south, not the north, but it states the same cost. From this I infer that holding a conquered area required troops who themselves needed supplies from the same distant base.

**Manpower and political strain**

- Chen Shou judged that Zhuge Liang's campaigns were not successful: "然連年動眾，未能成功，蓋應變將略，非其所長歟" (yet he moved the army year after year without success, perhaps because improvising tactics was not his strength) [38]. He also wrote that "攻守異體，故雖連年動眾，未能有克" (attacking and defending are different, so although he moved armies year after year, he could not win) [39].
- Later Jiang Wei was limited by Fei Yi, who "裁製不從，與其兵不過萬人" (restrained him, and his forces did not exceed ten thousand men) [32]. After Jiang Wei was defeated at Duan Valley, "眾庶由是怨讟，而隴以西亦騷動不寧" (the people blamed him, and the area west of Longshan was also unsettled) [33]. Sun Sheng's 《異同記》 records that Jiang Wei's critics said he "好戰無功，國內疲弊" (fought often without success, and the country was exhausted) [37].
- Wei's 景元四年 edict claimed Shu was exhausted by labor: "刻剥衆羌，勞役無已，民不堪命" (Jiang Wei squeezed the Qiang, the labor never ended, and the people could not bear the orders) [47]. This is Wei's own account, so treat it as one side's claim.

**Taken together:** Each advance from Shu lengthened a supply line that ran over mountain roads, and the records repeatedly show withdrawal when grain ran out. The conquered commanderies had only recently rebelled and were not firmly held. Holding them would have required garrisons that also needed grain, and Shu's manpower was limited. From these records I infer that a battle won at the front did not give Shu a base it could keep. This is an inference from the supply and garrison records, not a statement the sources make in one sentence.

q: Identify the stratagem: Wang Yun used Diaochan to sow suspicion between Dong Zhuo and Lü Bu, and in the end had Dong Zhuo killed by Lü Bu's hand. What is this stratagem usually called?
reply:
**Short answer:** The general name is **离间计** (*líjiàn jì*, "sowing discord"). The Diaochan element is usually called **美人计** ("beauty trap"), and the whole story as told in popular tradition is called **连环计**. These names come from later popular tradition, not from the *Sanguozhi*.

**What the *Sanguozhi* records:** The official history does not mention Diaochan. Several searches for 貂蝉 found only an unrelated court title, in Wei Yao's (韦曜) biography in the Wu section. What the text does record is that Wang Yun (王允) and Shi Sunrui (士孙瑞) secretly plotted to kill Dong Zhuo, and that they used Lü Bu as the inside man[1]. When Lü Bu objected that killing Dong Zhuo would betray a father-son bond, Wang Yun replied「君自姓呂，本非骨肉」[1], "You are surnamed Lü and were never of the same blood." Lü Bu agreed and personally stabbed Dong Zhuo: 「布遂許之，手刃刺卓」[1]. Dong Zhuo had earlier sworn to be Lü Bu's father「誓為父子」[4].

The killing took place at court. Lü Bu had Li Su and others, disguised as guards, strike Dong Zhuo, and「布曰『有詔』」, then「遂殺卓，夷三族」[6]. In other words, Lü Bu said there was an imperial edict, then killed Dong Zhuo and exterminated his three kin groups.

The records also show friction between the two men. Lü Bu「與卓侍婢私通，恐事發覺，心不自安」[3], "had an affair with one of Dong Zhuo's maids and feared discovery." Dong Zhuo once「拔手戟擲布」[3], threw a halberd at him, and Lü Bu dodged it. A note citing the *Yingxiong Ji* says a Daoist wrote the character 呂 and showed it to Dong Zhuo, who did not realize it meant Lü Bu[14]. Chen Shou's own assessment calls Lü Bu「輕狡反覆，唯利是視」[30], "fickle, treacherous, and interested only in profit."

**What this means:** From these records, it is reasonable to infer that Lü Bu's resentment of Dong Zhuo and his personal ties to him made him willing to turn, and that Wang Yun's argument about the bond settled the matter. This is my inference from [1], [3], and [4]. The records do not say anyone deliberately used a woman to set the two men against each other. The Diaochan scheme as a planned stratagem is not in the *Sanguozhi* and comes from later popular tradition.

q: Changban: who rescued the infant A'dou at Changban Slope? And who stood on Changban Bridge and scared off Cao Cao's army with his shouts?
reply:
**Short answer:** Zhao Yun rescued the infant A'dou, who was the child later known as Liu Shan, the Later Lord. Zhang Fei held the bridge at Changban against the pursuers.

**Zhao Yun and A'dou:** Cao Cao's cavalry caught Liu Bei at Changban Slope, and Liu Bei fled south leaving his wife and children behind. Zhao Yun's biography says 「雲身抱弱子，即後主也，保護甘夫人，即後主母也，皆得免難」[1]. In English: Zhao Yun personally held the young boy, who was the Later Lord, and protected Lady Gan, the Later Lord's mother, and both escaped. The biography of Lady Gan says the same: she was left behind during the pursuit and 「賴趙雲保護，得免於難」[22]. Pei Songzhi's note on Liu Shan's age also identifies the child Zhao Yun carried as Liu Shan, and dates the Changban defeat to 建安十三年 [21]. The sources use 「弱子」 and 「後主」 rather than the name A'dou.

**Zhang Fei and the bridge:** When Liu Bei learned that Cao Cao had arrived, he abandoned his wife and children and fled, and 「使飛將二十騎拒後」 [12]. Zhang Fei 「據水斷橋，瞋目橫矛曰：『身是張益德也，可來共決死！』敵皆無敢近者，故遂得免」[12]. In English: he held the river, cut the bridge, glared and levelled his spear, and shouted, "I am Zhang Yide! Come and fight to the death!" No enemy dared come near, and Liu Bei was able to escape. The text says the enemy did not dare approach. It does not say in so many words that Cao Cao's army turned back, though "scared off" is a fair reading of that result.

q: Sequence of episodes: put the following in the order in which they occur in *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*: A. The Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage  B. The Battle of Guandu  C. The Oath of the Peach Garden  D. The Battle of Red Cliffs
reply:
In *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (三国演义), the order is **C → B → A → D**: the Oath of the Peach Garden, the Battle of Guandu, the Three Visits to the Thatched Cottage, then the Battle of Red Cliffs. This is the novel's arrangement. The sources I searched cover only the *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (三国志) and its commentary, so I could not check the novel's order against them.

The *Records* do not match this sequence exactly:

- **Peach Garden:** The passages I found do not describe a formal oath. They say that Liu Bei 「先主與二人寢則同床，恩若兄弟」 ("slept on the same bed with the two of them, and their affection was like brothers") with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei [1].
- **Guandu:** The *Records* describe the campaign under 「五年春正月」 ("the first month of the fifth year") [27]. Yuan Shao's army was defeated: 「紹軍大潰，河北平」 ("Shao's army was routed, and Hebei was pacified") [28].
- **Three Visits:** Zhuge Liang's biography says that Liu Bei 「凡三往，乃見」 ("went to see him three times before meeting him") [16]. At that time Liu Bei 「屯新野」 was stationed at Xinye [16]. Zhuge Liang's memorial says Liu Bei 「三顧臣於草廬之中」 ("visited me three times in the thatched cottage") [11]. The *Records* give no year for the visits. The *Wei Lue* (《魏略》) says instead that 「亮乃北行見備」 ("Zhuge Liang went north to see Liu Bei") [21]. Pei Songzhi notes that these accounts conflict [11].
- **Red Cliffs:** The *Records* say 「與曹公戰於赤壁，大破之，焚其舟船」 ("fought Cao Cao at Red Cliffs, utterly defeated him, and burned his ships") [35].

q: Borrowing Arrows with Straw Boats: what weather conditions did Zhuge Liang take advantage of when he borrowed the arrows, and why did those conditions help him carry out the plan?
reply:
The records here do not show Zhuge Liang borrowing arrows with straw boats, and they do not mention fog or any weather as part of such a plan. Zhuge Liang's biography opens with his early life and his meeting with Liu Bei [3], and it does not describe this episode. The arrow-borrowing story is popularly linked to the novel 《三國演義》, but the sources I can consult do not include it, so I cannot say what the novel's version of the weather was.

The closest record is about Sun Quan, not Zhuge Liang. In a note citing 《吳歷》, Sun Quan went out in a large boat to observe Cao Cao's camp at 濡須. Cao Cao ordered his crossbowmen to fire, and the note records 「箭著其船，船偏重將覆」 (arrows struck the boat, it listed heavily and nearly capsized). Sun Quan turned his boat and 「復以一面受箭，箭均船平，乃還」 (took the arrows on the other side, the load evened out, and he returned) [18]. The 《魏略》 part of the same note gives the arrow detail, and it also gives no weather [18].

The only environmental detail in that note is Sun Quan's letter to Cao Cao: 「春水方生，公宜速去」 (spring water is rising, you should leave soon) [18]. That is a remark about the river level, not a description of a tactic, and it says nothing about fog.

So the sources cannot answer which weather conditions were used or why they would have helped. Any account of fog as the key condition would come from the novel, not from the *Sanguozhi* and its commentary.

q: Huarong Trail: in the novel, why does Guan Yu let Cao Cao go at Huarong Trail? What conflict within his character does this episode bring out?
reply:
In 《三国志》 there is no Huarong Trail scene in which Guan Yu lets Cao Cao go. That episode comes from 《三国演义》. The records do contain a real Cao Cao escape by the Huarong road, and a real relationship between Guan Yu and Cao Cao that shows the tension the novel dramatizes.

The only Huarong passage is a note to 《武帝纪》 citing 《山阳公载记》. It says Cao Cao retreated on foot along the Huarong road, where mud and wind blocked the way, and had his weakened soldiers fill the road with grass so the cavalry could pass. Afterward he said of Liu Bei, 「劉備，吾儔也。但得計少晚；向使早放火，吾徒無類矣。」[14] Guan Yu is not named in this account, and I found no record that he released Cao there.

Guan Yu's dealings with Cao are recorded in several places. After Cao captured him and treated him generously, Guan Yu told Zhang Liao, 「吾極知曹公待我厚，然吾受劉將軍厚恩，誓以共死，不可背之。」[1] He added, 「吾終不留，吾要當立效以報曹公乃去。」[1] He killed Yan Liang, sealed up Cao's gifts, and went to Yuan Shao's camp to rejoin Liu Bei. Cao's men wanted to pursue him, but Cao said, 「彼各為其主，勿追也。」[1] A note citing 《傅子》 has Cao call him 「事君不忘其本，天下義士也」.[3]

A note citing 《蜀記》 says that when Liu Bei and Cao hunted together in Xu, Guan Yu urged Liu Bei to kill Cao, and Liu Bei refused.[8] Pei Songzhi doubts this account, arguing that Liu Bei was then plotting with Dong Cheng against Cao.[8]

Chen Shou's closing judgment on Guan Yu reads: 「羽報效曹公，飛義釋嚴顏，並有國士之風。然羽剛而自矜，飛暴而無恩，以短取敗，理數之常也。」[18]

The conflict the records show is between loyalty to Liu Bei and gratitude to Cao. Guan Yu had sworn to die with Liu Bei, but he also owed Cao a debt. The record shows him resolving this by repaying Cao's favors (killing Yan Liang, sealing up the gifts) before leaving, rather than staying or betraying Liu Bei. Chen Shou's judgment points to a character flaw in the same area: Guan Yu was proud and unyielding (「剛而自矜」), which Chen Shou sees as the cause of his downfall. The novel's Huarong scene dramatizes the same debt, with Guan Yu sparing Cao out of gratitude for past kindness. That is the novel's version, which I could not check against the records.

q: The chained ships: before the Battle of Red Cliffs, who advised Ts'ao Ts'ao to link his warships together with iron chains? Why did this arrangement magnify the damage done by the fire attack?
reply:
The records I found do not name anyone who advised Cao Cao to chain his warships together, and they do not mention iron chains. The only description of the linked fleet is Huang Gai's remark that Cao's warships were joined end to end. Pang Tong's biography, as far as I read it, says nothing about Cao's fleet [11][34]. The Pang Tong attribution is therefore not supported by these sources.

Zhou Yu's biography records Huang Gai's argument: 「今寇眾我寡，難與持久。然觀操軍船艦，首尾相接，可燒而走也。」 ("The enemy is numerous and we are few, so we cannot hold out for long. But I see that Cao's warships are joined head to tail; they can be burned and the enemy driven off.") [3]. Huang Gai is credited with proposing the fire attack at Red Cliffs [24]. The text says the ships were joined, but it does not say who ordered this or why.

The records also do not say outright that the linking made the fire worse. The following is my inference from them.

- The fire ships were sent into the fleet with a strong wind behind them. The Jiangbiao zhuan (cited in Zhou Yu's biography) says: 「火烈風猛，往船如箭，飛埃絕爛，燒盡北船，延及岸邊營柴」 ("The fire was fierce and the wind strong; the burning ships shot forward like arrows, the flying embers spread everywhere, the northern ships were burned out, and the fire reached the camp's firewood on the bank") [19].
- Zhou Yu's biography adds that the wind spread the flames through the shore camps: 「時風盛猛，悉延燒岸上營落」 [3].
- Because the ships were joined head to tail [3], one burning vessel could pass fire to the next, and the wind carried it across the whole formation. This suggests that the linking helped the fire spread from ship to ship. The records do not show that crews were unable to cut the ships apart. Huang Gai's ships were also set up to look like surrendering vessels, so Cao's men were watching them approach [3].

Other points in the records explain why Cao's fleet was vulnerable, though they do not concern the linking. Zhuge Liang said 「北方之人，不習水戰」 ("people from the north are not used to naval warfare") [2]. Zhou Yu's biography says 「曹公軍眾已有疾病」 ("Cao's army was already suffering from disease") [3].

q: Identify the posthumous ruse: in the saying 'a dead Zhuge frightens off a living Zhongda', who is 'Zhongda'? In the novel, how does the Shu army make him retreat?
reply:
**Answer:** "Zhongda" is **Sima Yi (司马懿)**, whose courtesy name was Zhongda (仲达). The sources usually call him Sima Xuanwang (司马宣王). The saying refers to his withdrawal after Zhuge Liang died during the Wuzhangyuan campaign, in 建兴十二年 (the twelfth year of the Jianxing era of Shu).

**The saying.** Pei Songzhi's commentary quotes the *Han-Jin Chunqiu* (《汉晋春秋》): when Sima Yi withdrew, the common people made a saying, 「死諸葛走生仲達」[1], roughly "the dead Zhuge put the living Zhongda to flight." When this was reported to him, Sima Yi replied, 「吾能料生，不便料死也」[1], "I can predict the living, but I cannot predict the dead."

**How the Shu army made him retreat.** The main text says Zhuge Liang died at the camp, and his army withdrew [3][6]. The *Han-Jin Chunqiu* account gives the sequence. Yang Yi led the army out, and the people ran to tell Sima Yi, who pursued [1]. Jiang Wei then had Yang Yi turn the banners and beat the drums, as if about to attack Sima Yi. Sima Yi withdrew and 「不敢偪」[1], "did not dare to press closer." Yang Yi formed up and left, and only after entering the valley did the army announce Zhuge's death, 「入谷然後發喪」[1]. The retreat was therefore a bluff: the Shu army looked as though it would fight, and Sima Yi did not test it.

**The novel.** The sources I searched do not include *Romance of the Three Kingdoms* (《三国演义》), so I cannot confirm from them how the novel tells this episode. The novel's version is widely known to involve a wooden effigy of Zhuge Liang, but I have not verified that against the text here, so treat it as unconfirmed.

q: Arrange 'county, province, commandery' from highest to lowest according to the usual local administrative hierarchy of the late Eastern Han.
reply:
**Answer: province (州) > commandery (郡) > county (縣).**

- **Province (州), highest.** The sources describe the province-level 刺史 as governing the commanderies. Chen Shou's comment on the Wei biographies says: 「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已。」[1] ("Since the late Han, the Inspectors (刺史) have governed the commanderies as a whole and administered affairs outside the capital, not merely inspecting them as in earlier times.") Biographies also show the two posts as separate: 常林 was promoted to 博陵太守 and then 幽州刺史.[7]

- **Commandery (郡), middle.** Commanderies sat between the province and the counties. 賈逵 was made 豫州刺史, and the source says the province was originally sent out to inspect the 「長吏二千石已下」 (officials of the 2,000-bushel rank and below).[8] A memorial attributed to 夏侯玄 (Xiahou Xuan) describes the commandery's role as 「職監諸縣」 (to supervise the counties).[10] In the 賀齊 biography, 「郡發屬縣五千兵，各使本縣長將之」 (the commandery drew 5,000 troops from its subordinate counties, each led by that county's chief).[16]

- **County (縣), lowest.** Counties were the base unit, headed by a 縣令 or 縣長. 常林 was made 縣長 and served as magistrate of 南和.[7] The same memorial's proposal to abolish commanderies refers to counties under 「千戶以下令長如故」 (magistrates and chiefs for counties of under 1,000 households remain as before),[10] which suggests the title depended on county size, though it does not spell out the rule.

From [1], the province began as a supervisory circuit rather than a fixed administrative tier. By the late Han it had become a governing level above the commanderies. That is my inference from the comment, not a separate statement in the sources.

q: Empty Fort Strategy: in the novel, where does Zhuge Liang use the Empty Fort Strategy, and which Wei commander leads the army that comes against him?
reply:
The Empty Fort (空城计) is a scene from the novel *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, and the commander is Sima Yi (司马懿). I found no account of that scene in the *Records of the Three Kingdoms*. The closest story there also names Sima Yi as the Wei commander, but it is set at Yangping (阳平), not in a northern city.

In the novel, Zhuge Liang sits at Xicheng (西城) with almost no troops, opens the gates, and Sima Yi retreats, suspecting an ambush. The *Records* does mention Xicheng, but only as a route. Sima Yi was to advance by Xicheng in Jianxing 8, along with Zhang He and Cao Zhen, and 「丞相亮待之於城固、赤坂，大雨道絕，真等皆還」 [27] ("the Chancellor Liang waited for them at Chenggu and Chibi, heavy rain cut the roads, and Cao Zhen and the others all withdrew"). No gate-opening appears there.

The nearest parallel is in Pei Songzhi's annotation to Zhuge Liang's biography, quoting Guo Chong's *Sanshi* (《三事》). Zhuge Liang is at Yangping with only 10,000 men in the city. Sima Yi, who commands 200,000, reports that the city is weak. Zhuge Liang 「又令大開四城門，埽地卻洒」 [1] ("had all four city gates opened, and the ground swept and sprinkled"). Sima Yi 「疑其有伏兵，於是引軍北趣山」 [1] ("suspected an ambush and led his army north toward the mountains"). Zhuge Liang laughs and says 「司馬懿必謂吾怯，將有彊伏，循山走矣」 [1] ("Sima Yi must think I am timid and that there is a strong ambush, so he has gone off along the mountains").

Pei Songzhi disputes this account. He notes that Yangping is in Hanzhong, and that Sima Yi was then Governor of Jingzhou based at Wan (宛城) [1]. He also says there is no other record of fighting at Yangping [1]. He asks 「若疑其有伏兵，正可設防持重，何至便走乎」 [1] ("If he suspected an ambush, he could have set up defenses and held his ground. Why would he flee?"). Pei judges that this book's citations are false: 「故知此書舉引皆虛」 [20] ("so we know the citations in this book are all false"). Shu's annals do place Zhuge Liang at the Yangping camp in Jianxing 5 [10], but that does not confirm the gate story.

What the *Records* does describe is a long standoff in the Northern Expeditions. Chen Shou writes: 「司馬宣王與亮相持，連圍積日，亮數挑戰，宣王堅壘不應。會亮卒，其軍退還」 [9] ("Sima Xuan faced Liang for many days. Liang challenged him repeatedly, but Sima Xuan held his fortified camp and did not respond. When Liang died, his army withdrew"). The Wei emperor had ordered Sima Yi to hold his walls and wait for Shu to run out of supplies [16]. Chen Shou's assessment of Zhuge Liang's campaigns is 「然連年動眾，未能成功，蓋應變將略，非其所長歟」 [22] ("Yet he mobilized armies year after year without success. Perhaps flexible tactics in the field were not his strength"). No ruse like the Empty Fort is mentioned.

In short, the Empty Fort is a novel scene with Sima Yi as the Wei commander. The *Records* does not contain that scene, though its Yangping gate-opening story, which Pei Songzhi rejects, also has Sima Yi as commander.

q: In the late Eastern Han, was a 'Grand Administrator' (taishou) normally the chief official of a province, a commandery or a county?
reply:
A Grand Administrator (太守, *taishou*) normally headed a **commandery (郡)**. He was not the head of a province or a county. Provinces were headed by an Inspector (刺史), and counties by a magistrate (縣長 or 縣令).

**Commandery:** Shi Xie had his brother appointed as Grand Administrator of Hepu: 「燮乃表壹領合浦太守」 [1]. When Sun Ce took Kuaiji, 「策自領會稽太守」 ("Ce took the post of Grand Administrator of Kuaiji himself"), and he then named others to the commanderies of Danyang, Yuzhang and Wu [15]. Pei Qian was appointed 「以潛爲代郡太守」 ("made Grand Administrator of Dai Commandery") when Dai was in great disorder [17].

**Province:** The province was headed by an Inspector, as in 「益州刺史郤儉」 ("Inspector of Yi Province, Xi Jian") [8], and 「交州刺史」 appears for the southern province [7]. Liu Yan was later 「領益州牧」 ("concurrently Governor of Yi Province") [8]. The sources name Grand Administrators and Inspectors as separate posts but do not spell out their chain of command in one sentence.

**County:** Liu Yao was 「除下邑長」 ("appointed Chief of Xiayi County") [5], and Chang Lin 「林宰南和」 ("served as magistrate of Nanhe") [2]. Chang Lin was later 「超遷博陵太守」 ("promoted over the usual steps to Grand Administrator of Boling") [2]. This promotion from county magistrate to Grand Administrator suggests, by inference, that the Grand Administrator ranked above the county magistrate.

The record for the Wei agricultural colonies is a further example. It reads 「諸典農皆為太守，都尉皆為令長」 ("each chief of the agricultural colonies became a Grand Administrator, and each colonel became a magistrate or chief") [13]. From this, one can infer that 太守 was a commandery-level post and 令長 a county-level one. This is a Wei-era measure, and the record does not give its year.

q: Both the 'Inspector' (cishi) and the 'Governor' (zhoumu) were offices tied to the province. What was the Inspector's original main function? And why can't every Inspector of the late Eastern Han simply be regarded as an official with supervisory powers only?
reply:
The Inspector (刺史) began as a supervisory envoy. By the late Eastern Han it had become a regional authority with administrative and military power, so it cannot be treated as purely supervisory.

**The original function was inspection.** Jia Kui (贾逵) describes the province as a Censorate commission: 「州本以御史出監諸郡，以六條詔書察長吏二千石已下」[5]. Inspectors checked officials of 2,000 bushels and below against the Six Articles. Sima Yi's reply in the Xiahou Xuan (夏侯玄) biography says the Han Inspector 「奉六條而已」, that his staff were called 「從事」, that he had 「居無常治」 (no fixed seat), and that the office only later became a formal bureau: 「其後轉更爲官司耳」[3]. Xiahou Xuan himself proposed abolishing the commandery governors and keeping only the Inspectors, reasoning that 「刺史職存，則監察不廢」[1]. Even in the third century, supervision was still the stated core of the office.

**Why the office outgrew supervision.** Several records show this:

- Chen Shou's appraisal at the end of the Wei shu biographies of Liu, Sima, Liang, Zhang, Wen and Jia says that 「自漢季以来，刺史總統諸郡，賦政于外，非若曩時司察之而已」[4]. Since the late Han, Inspectors governed the commanderies and ran administration outside the capital, which he contrasts with the earlier role of inspection alone.
- Inspectors commanded troops. Tao Qian was appointed Inspector of Xuzhou and 「擊黃巾，破走之」[21]. Niu Zhao (牵招) said that Gao Gan, Inspector of Bingzhou, had 「帶甲五萬」 under him, a strong base[16]. Du Shu (杜恕), son of Du Ji (杜畿), proposed that Inspectors should 「勿令領兵，以專民事」[2]. That proposal assumes they did command troops in his time.
- The Inspector and Governor (牧) titles were held by the same kind of men. Liu Yan was 「出為監軍使者，領益州牧」[12]. The Xu Hanshu (续汉书) says that Liu Biao was made Inspector of Jingzhou and Jia Cong Inspector of Jizhou, and that men chosen as 「牧伯」 from the ministries 「各以本秩居任」[11]. Pei Songzhi's note adds that Liu Biao's appointment to Jingzhou was not at the same time as Liu Yan's[11]. The sources therefore do not give a single reform date or edict that turned Inspectors into Governors.

From these records, I infer that the title Inspector by the late Eastern Han covered both the older supervisory role and real administrative and military command. Inspectors who held troops and governed their territory, like Tao Qian and Gao Gan, cannot be explained by supervision alone. This is an inference from the passages above, not a direct statement in any single source.

q: Chu-ko Liang was Chancellor of Shu-Han and also held the charge of 'Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat' (lu shangshu shi). Taking part in and overseeing what kind of business did that charge chiefly mean?
reply:
Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat (錄尚書事) meant supervising the business of the Secretariat (尚書台), the central office that handled state documents and affairs. The sources never define the title in a single sentence, so this description is drawn from how it is used.

When Liu Bei made Zhuge Liang Chancellor, the record says 「亮以丞相錄尚書事，假節」 ("Liang, as Chancellor, recorded the affairs of the Secretariat, and was given a symbol of authority") [2]. Under Liu Shan, 「政事無巨細，咸決於亮」 ("state affairs, large or small, were all decided by Liang") [3]. Later holders used related wording. After Zhuge Liang died, Dong Jue became Shangshu Ling and was made 「平台事」 ("to settle the affairs of the Secretariat") [5]. Zhuge Zhan 「與輔國大將軍南鄉侯董厥并平尚書事」 ("together with Dong Jue, settled the affairs of the Secretariat") in the Jingyao era [28]. Jiang Wan was made 「錄尚書事」 after Zhuge Liang's death [1].

Wei records show the same pattern. A Wei edict, quoted in the 《魏略》 note, planned that one official would be in charge of 「錄後臺文書事」 ("recording the documents of the rear office") and another of 「錄行尚書事」 ("recording the Secretariat's business while in motion"). That was a conditional plan for when the emperor was on campaign [15]. Chen Qun 「錄尚書事」 [14]. Wu Zhi later criticized him for 「處重任而不親事」 ("holding a heavy post but not handling affairs personally") [19].

From these records, I infer that 錄尚書事 gave its holder overall supervision of the Secretariat's documents, rulings and daily administration, with the chancellor or senior minister as the final decider. This is why Zhuge Liang's record says all administrative affairs were decided by him [3]. The Wei criticism of Chen Qun suggests the post was expected to involve handling business, not just holding the title. The sources do not list the formal duties in full, so these points are inference, not explicit definition.

q: In the title 'Marquis of Hanshou Village' (Hanshou tinghou), is 'Marquis' an office or a rank of nobility? Did Guan Yu's receiving this title mean that he served as Prefect of Hanshou county?
reply:
**Short answer:** "Marquis" (侯) is a noble rank, not an office. Receiving the title did not make Guan Yu Prefect of Hanshou. None of the passages I found say he governed Hanshou.

**Rank, not office.** After the battle of Baima, the text says 「曹公即表封羽為漢壽亭侯」 ("Cao Cao immediately petitioned to enfeoff Yu as Marquis of Hanshou Village") [1]. The verb 封 ("enfeoff") is the one used for granting noble titles. Other entries use the same wording: Yu Jin was made 「封益壽亭侯」 [8], and Quan Cong was made 「於是封陽華亭侯」 after advising on an attack on Guan Yu [2]. The commentary on Guan Yu's biography, quoting 《傅子》 and Pei Songzhi's note, deals with Cao Cao's decision to let him leave, not with any post at Hanshou [13][14].

**No prefecture at Hanshou.** The sources record two administrative posts for Guan Yu, and neither is Hanshou:
- When Liu Bei killed the Xuzhou Governor Che Zhou, he 「使羽守下邳城，行太守事」 ("had Yu guard Xiapi city and act as Prefect") [5]. This was an acting post at Xiapi.
- After Liu Bei took the southern commanderies, he 「以羽為襄陽太守、蕩寇將軍」 ("made Yu Prefect of Xiangyang and General Who Sweeps the Bandits") [25].

Chen Shou's closing assessment of Guan Yu does not mention Hanshou [21].

**Limits.** The idea that a 亭侯 held no governing role is general background on the rank system, not something stated in any passage I found. The sources record the title and the posts above, but they do not say how the Hanshou fief was administered.

q: Which present-day city roughly corresponds to Jianye of the Three Kingdoms period? What is the city that served as Shu-Han's capital called today?
reply:
**Jianye** corresponds to present-day **Nanjing** in Jiangsu. The capital of Shu-Han was **Chengdu** in Sichuan.

**Jianye.** The sources say Sun Quan moved his seat to Moling (秣陵) in the sixteenth year of the Jian'an era, and the following year built a city at Shitou and renamed Moling as Jianye: 「權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業。」[1] The "following year" is Jian'an 17, which is 公元212年. Sun Quan later moved his seat to Jianye again: 「秋九月，權遷都建業」[4]. In between, he had made Wuchang his capital: 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」[6]. The identification of Jianye with Nanjing is my general knowledge, not something the sources state.

**Shu-Han.** Liu Bei took the imperial title 「即皇帝位於成都武擔之南」[15] in Jian'an 26, which is 公元221年. After his death, Liu Shan 「襲位於成都」[11]. Chengdu had already been the seat of Liu Yan's administration, since Liu Yan 「徙治成都」[27]. The modern identification of Chengdu is my general knowledge.

q: Which cities normally served as the capitals of Ts'ao-Wei, Shu-Han and Sun-Wu respectively? For Wu, give the capital used over the long term after Sun Ch'üan moved the court.
reply:
**Short answer:** Wei's capital was Luoyang, Shu-Han's was Chengdu, and Wu's long-term capital was Jianye (建業, near modern Nanjing). Sun Quan moved the court to Wuchang for a time, then returned to Jianye.

**Wei (Luoyang).** The record says 「十二月，初營洛陽宮，戊午幸洛陽」 [6] ("In the twelfth month the palace at Luoyang was first built, and on the day wuwu the ruler went to Luoyang"), and Cao Pi's father Cao Cao died there: 「庚子，王崩于洛陽」 [7]. Luoyang had been damaged earlier, and 「洛陽殘破，董昭等勸太祖都許」 [1] ("Luoyang was ruined, and Dong Zhao and others urged Cao Cao to make Xu the capital"), so Cao Cao 「奉迎天子都許」 [8] ("welcomed the emperor and made Xu the capital"). The 《魏略》, cited in the annotation to Cao Pi's annals, lists five 都: 「改長安、譙、許昌、鄴、洛陽爲五都」 [5]. By inference, Luoyang was the city where Cao Pi built the palace and where Cao Cao died, but the 《魏略》 passage shows Wei designated several major cities rather than one fixed capital.

**Shu-Han (Chengdu).** Liu Bei took Chengdu by siege: 「十九年夏，雒城破，進圍成都數十日，璋出降」 [17] ("In summer of the nineteenth year, Luocheng fell, he besieged Chengdu for several dozen days, and Liu Zhang surrendered"). He then 「取蜀城中金銀分賜將士」 [17] and took the title 益州牧 again. Chengdu remained the base: 「先主亦還成都」 [19] ("the former ruler also returned to Chengdu"), and 「十二月，亮還成都」 [12] ("in the twelfth month Liang returned to Chengdu"). The passages do not give a separate formal decree naming Chengdu as the capital, but they consistently treat it as the seat of government.

**Wu (Jianye).** Sun Quan first moved his seat to Moling: 「十六年，權徙治秣陵。明年，城石頭，改秣陵爲建業」 [29] ("In the sixteenth year, Quan moved his seat to Moling. The next year he built the stone fortress and renamed Moling as Jianye"). Later, after Liu Bei had proclaimed himself emperor, 「權自公安都鄂，改名武昌」 [28] ("Quan moved from Gong'an to E and renamed it Wuchang"). The move to Jianye came after that: 「黃龍元年，權遷都建業」 [24] ("In the first year of Huanglong, Quan moved the capital to Jianye"), and 「秋九月，權遷都建業，因固府不改館」 [22] ("In the autumn of the ninth month, Quan moved the capital to Jianye, keeping the existing offices without changing the buildings"). Wuchang was therefore a seat used for a period, while Jianye was the capital Wu settled on.

q: Jiange chiefly controls traffic between which two regions? Why is it so well suited to defense?
reply:
**Answer:** Jiange controlled the road between **Hanzhong** in the north and the **Chengdu plain (Yi Province, Shu's heartland)** in the south. The sources do not describe the pass's physical terrain, so its defensive strength has to be inferred from how the campaign of 263 unfolded.

**The two regions.** Yang Hong told Zhuge Liang that Hanzhong was the key to Yi Province: 「漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會」 [25]. Wei's invasion route ran through Hanzhong. Zhong Hui's main army 「分從斜谷、駱谷入」 [21], and Jiang Wei then 「還守劍閣」 [1]. Deng Ai's bypass proposal shows where Jiange sat: he wanted to 「出劍閣西百里，去成都三百餘里」 [1], which puts the pass between the two regions.

**Why it was hard to take.** The sources give three points.

- **It stopped a much larger army.** Zhong Hui's forces 「進攻劍閣，不克，引退，蜀軍保險拒守」 [2]. Pei Songzhi wrote that at Jiange 「維與諸將列營守險，會不得進」 [6]. The *Yuan Zi* (quoted in the commentary) says Zhong Hui held Jiange with 「二十萬眾」 but 「不得進」 [9].
- **Its supply lines were long.** The attackers faced 「糧運縣遠，將議還歸」 [30], and Zhong Hui considered withdrawing.
- **It fell only when bypassed.** Deng Ai did not break Jiange. He 「自陰平由景谷道傍入，遂破諸葛瞻於綿竹」 [30], and 「艾遂至綿竹，大戰，斬諸葛瞻」 [2]. Pei Songzhi notes that once Deng Ai took this route, 「諸葛瞻既敗，成都自潰」 [6].

**Inference.** From these passages, the pass worked as a block on the main road from Hanzhong to Chengdu. It could hold off a force several times the size of its garrison, and it forced the attacker either to fight a costly siege or to find a sidepath. Wei succeeded only by the sidepath, which turned Jiange's defenders' position into a liability once Zhuge Zhan's force at Mianzhu was defeated. Because Jiang Wei's army was still at Jiange when Chengdu fell, the sources do not show that the pass itself was ever breached.

**Caveat.** The sources call Jiange 「險」 and 「險要」 (dangerous, strategically vital), but they do not describe its gorge, road, or cliffs. Any account of the terrain itself would have to come from outside these records.

q: Can the 'Jing Province' of the late Eastern Han be equated directly with today's Jingzhou city in Hubei? Explain how the two differ as geographical concepts.
reply:
No. In the late Eastern Han, Jing Province (荆州) was a regional unit (州) that contained several commanderies (郡). Modern Jingzhou is a single city-level unit inside the area that was once that province.

**Jing Province was a region of many commanderies.** The sources describe its extent piecemeal. Liu Biao (刘表) 「南收零、桂，北據漢川，地方數千里，帶甲十餘萬」[13] ("took Lingling and Guiyang to the south, held the Han River region to the north; the territory covered several thousand *li* and had over 100,000 armoured troops"). Lingling and Guiyang are commanderies, and the text places them within his reach. A strategist quoted in the commentary says 「荊州八郡可傳檄而定」[17] ("the eight commanderies of Jing Province could be pacified by a single proclamation"). The passage does not list the eight. Modern Hunan and Hubei lie in the area, but that geographical identification is my own general knowledge, not something the sources state.

**Nanyang's status is unclear from the sources.** Yuan Shu (袁术) 「術得據其郡」[7] ("was able to hold that commandery" after Sun Jian killed the Nanyang governor), and he tried to seize Liu Biao's province: 「欲襲奪表州」[13]. This suggests Nanyang was not under Liu Biao's control at that time. The sources do not say whether it was formally part of Jing Province.

**The province was defined by its inspector and governor, not a city.** Before Liu Biao, the office was 荊州刺史, and 「代王叡為荊州刺史」[12] ("succeeded Wang Rui as Jing Province inspector"). Later it was 荊州牧 (governor). Sun Jian had earlier killed Wang Rui on his way to Nanyang: 「荊州刺史王睿素遇堅無禮，堅過殺之」[1]. The office was tied to a region, not to one seat.

**The province's bases moved.** Liu Qi (刘琮) 「屯襄陽」[11] ("garrisoned Xiangyang"), and Liu Bei (刘备) 「屯樊」[11] ("was at Fan"). After Cao Cao (曹操) took the region, he 「進軍江陵，下令荊州吏民」[11] ("advanced on Jiangling and issued an order to the officials and people of Jing Province"). Later Liu Bei 「領荊州牧，屯公安」[22] ("held the post of Jing Province governor and was stationed at Gong'an"). Xiangyang, Jiangling, and Gong'an were each a base at different times. None was the province as a whole.

**The province was split between two states.** Around the time Liu Bei gained Yi Province (益州), Sun Quan and Liu Bei divided the land: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」[20] ("the parts of Jing Province east of Jiangxia, Changsha, and Guiyang went to the east, and Nanjun, Lingling, and Wuling went to the west"). After this, the name covered land under two regimes.

**Relation to modern Jingzhou.** Modern Jingzhou city is in south-central Hubei. Its historical core corresponds roughly to ancient Jiangling (江陵), which the sources name as a major base. That identification is general knowledge, not something the passages say. So modern Jingzhou is one city-level area within the historical region. It is not the same as Jing Province, which covered several commanderies and parts of what are now several provincial-level areas.

q: Is Hanzhong north or south of the Qinling mountains? Why was it such an important region for Shu-Han, both for defending against attack from the north and for sending armies northward?
reply:
Hanzhong lies **south** of the Qinling. The sources don't give its position in one sentence, but their routes show it. Whoever held Hanzhong controlled the passes into Yi Province from the north, and from there Shu-Han could send armies north.

**Position.** Wei Yan proposed a raid that would go "直從褒中出，循秦嶺而東，當子午而北，不過十日可到長安" [6]. That route starts at Hanzhong, runs along the Qinling, and reaches Chang'an, so the mountains lie between them. Armies from Wei crossed the range to reach Hanzhong: Cao Cao's forces went "王自長安出斜谷，軍遮要以臨漢中" [7], and Cao Zhen's went "從子午道南入" [53]. By inference, invaders from Chang'an had to cross the Qinling through valleys such as Xie and Ziwu to reach Hanzhong.

**Defense.** Yang Hong called Hanzhong the key to Yi Province: "漢中則益州咽喉，存亡之機會，若無漢中則無蜀矣" [5]. In 建安二十年 Cao Cao took it: "公軍入南鄭，盡得魯府庫珍寶。巴、漢皆降" [27]. He then left Xiahou Yuan to hold it [24]. Liu Ye had urged an immediate attack, warning that if delayed, Shu would "據險守要，則不可犯矣" [3]. In 建安二十四年 Liu Bei defeated Xiahou Yuan at Dingjun Mountain. He then "斂眾拒險，終不交鋒，積月不拔" until Cao Cao withdrew, and so took Hanzhong [8]. Holding it was costly for Wei too. He Qia had advised moving the population, which "可省置守之費" [29]. Cao Cao did not accept, and Wei later gave up Hanzhong [29].

**Offense.** Fa Zheng argued that taking Hanzhong would let Shu "上可以傾覆寇敵，尊獎王室，中可以蠶食雍、涼，廣拓境土，下可以固守要害" [37]. Zhou Qun was more cautious: "當得其地，不得其民也" [14]. Zhuge Liang's northern campaigns began from Hanzhong. In 建興五年 he "率諸軍北駐漢中" [11], and in 建興六年 "亮身率諸軍攻祁山" [50]. He rejected Wei Yan's bold route, judging it better "不如安從坦道，可以平取隴右" [6]. In 建興十一年 supplies were "集於斜谷口" [55], and in 建興十二年 he left by Xie Valley [55]. His memorial, preserved in the Han-Jin Chunqiu, gives the strategic reason: "顧王業不得偏全於蜀都" and "然不伐賊，王業亦亡" [20].

After Zhuge Liang, Jiang Wei led repeated northern campaigns. Zhang Yi warned him, "可止矣，不宜復進" [44]. Jiang Wei won at Didao but could not take the city, and he dismissed the warning as "為蛇畫足" [44]. Fei Yi often restrained Jiang Wei's larger plans and kept his force to no more than 10,000 [48].

The same passes were the final weak point. In 景元四年 Zhong Hui's army "分從斜谷、駱谷入" [45], and Jiang Wei "遂東引，還守劍閣" [38]. Deng Ai then took a side route: "鄧艾自陰平由景谷道傍入，遂破諸葛瞻於綿竹" [47], and "艾遂至綿竹，大戰，斬諸葛瞻" [41].

Inference: the records show Hanzhong was valuable for two reasons. It shielded the Chengdu plain from attack, and it was the staging ground for northern campaigns. The same geography that made it defensible also meant that once an enemy held the Qinling passes or the Jiange defenses, the Shu heartland was exposed.

q: How does the Records of the Three Kingdoms tell the story of the "belt edict" (the secret edict hidden in Emperor Xian's belt), and why did Liu Bei not mention it when he proclaimed himself emperor?
reply:
Chen Shou tells the belt-edict story only briefly, and the record gives no reason for Liu Bei's silence. What it does show is that Liu Bei cited the Dong Cheng plot when he became King of Hanzhong, and left it out only when he proclaimed himself emperor. The explanation below is my inference from the texts.

**The story as recorded.** Before Liu Bei left Xu, the emperor's relative Dong Cheng received a secret edict from the emperor's belt: 「獻帝舅車騎將軍董承辭受帝衣帶中密詔，當誅曹公」 [1]. Liu Bei joined the plot, but 「先主未發」, he had not acted when it was discovered, and Dong Cheng and the others were executed [1]. The *Wei Shu* adds that before heading east Liu Bei 「陰與董承等謀反」, killed the Xuzhou governor at Xiapi, and raised troops at Pei [8]. The text never gives the edict's contents. Later, Empress Fu was deposed and killed after a letter was discovered saying the emperor resented Cao Cao over Dong Cheng's death [3].

**What he said when he became King of Hanzhong.** In 建安二十四年 he was made King of Hanzhong [19]. His own memorial states: 「臣昔與車騎將軍董承圖謀討操，機事不密，承見陷害，臣播越失據，忠義不果」 ("I once plotted with Dong Cheng to attack Cao Cao; the secret was not kept, Dong Cheng was caught and killed, and I fled and lost my base") [5]. The officials' petition also says he 「與車騎將軍董承同謀誅操」 [2]. So the plot was openly cited at this stage. The edict itself was not.

**The proclamation.** In 建安二十六年四月丙午 he took the throne at Chengdu [20]. The proclamation blames Cao Cao 「戮殺主後」 and Cao Pi 「載其凶逆，竊居神器」, and rests on the call of officials and the people: 「天命不可以不答，祖業不可以久替，四海不可以無主」 [20]. It does not mention Dong Cheng, the plot, or the edict. The petition before it argued that 「今上無天子，海內惶惶」 and relied on omens and charts [28]. The record also says that after Cao Pi took the throne, 「或傳聞漢帝見害，先主乃發喪制服，追諡曰孝愍皇帝」, so Liu Bei mourned the emperor as dead and gave him a posthumous title [24].

**Why he may have left it out (inference).**
- The petition's central claim was that there was no emperor on the throne [28]. A secret order from a living emperor would weaken that argument. The rumour of the emperor's death let him present the throne as empty [24].
- The proclamation's case rests on heaven, omens, and Cao family crimes [20][28]. The edict would have added a claim that the emperor had authorized his action, and the record does not show Liu Bei making that claim.
- In the Hanzhong memorial he treats the plot as a failure of secrecy, not as a credential for the throne [5].
- Sun Quan's reply to Liu Bei's later title, in the *Jiangbiao zhuan* commentary, shows the emperor's existence was itself a live argument: 「前所以名西爲蜀者，以漢帝尚存故耳，今漢已廢」 [44]. Liu Bei's advisers were arguing from the emperor's status, not from any order he had given.
- Objections to kingship focused on timing. Fei Shi said 「今天敵未克，而先主自立」 [46]. The record does not show anyone raising the edict in these debates.

These points explain why the edict would have been awkward to cite at the proclamation. They do not show what Liu Bei intended, and the record does not say.

q: Why was Sima Yi able to be enshrined in the Ancestral Temple of Cao Cao (to share in the sacrifices to the Wei founder)?
reply:
**Short answer:** The sources do not state a single reason. They record that in the eleventh month of Jiaping 3 (254), after Sima Yi's death in the seventh month, officials ranked the meritorious ministers due sacrifice in the Taizu (Cao Cao) temple by rank, and put him first because of his merit and rank. Why he qualified at all is not stated, so the rest is inference.

**What the record says.** The entry reads: 「有司奏諸功臣應饗食於太祖廟者，更以官為次，太傅司馬宣王功高爵尊，最在上」 [3]. Roughly: officials proposed that the meritorious ministers who should be honored in the Taizu temple be ordered by office, and the Grand Tutor Sima Xuanwang, "of high merit and high rank," stood at the top. The entry gives the ordering criterion, not the basis for inclusion.

**The general standard.** An edict quoted in the commentary, cited in connection with enshrining Xiahou Dun, says the sacrifice applied to 「大魏元功之臣功勳優著，終始休明者」, founding-merit ministers "whose achievements were outstanding and who were admirable from beginning to end" [8]. The sources do not say Sima Yi was a 元功之臣. By inference, his inclusion depends on whether he met this standard, and the record of his achievements is what would support that.

**His recorded merit.**
- On his deathbed, Emperor Ming told him 「君其與爽輔少子」, "you and Cao Shuang should together assist my young son" [15].
- He led the campaign against Gongsun Yuan. The Emperor said 「司馬懿臨危制變，擒淵可計日待也」 [12]. Gongsun Yuan and his son were executed, and the commanderies of the east were pacified [20]. Rewards were then given to the commanders, with Sima Yi named first [12].
- After the Gaoping Tomb coup, Jiang Ji's memorial praised 「太傅奮獨斷之策」, "the Grand Tutor's decisive plan" [32].
- He defeated Meng Da [23] and was ordered to resist Zhuge Liang [5].
- An edict of the Ming reign calls him 「太尉體履正直，功蓋海內」, "upright in conduct, with merit covering the realm" [10].

**Caveats.**
- Pei Songzhi questions the court's choices: why Xun Yu was not included, why Xu Chu was passed over in favor of Dian Wei, and why Guo Jia was left out while Cheng Yu was honored [1]. This suggests the selection did not follow a fully consistent rule.
- Praise for Sima Yi's great merit (「懿有大功，海內所書」) appears in a memorial by Guanqiu Jian and Wen Qin [11]. They wrote in revolt against Sima Shi, so their judgment is partisan. The court's own edict [10] and the entry on his rank [3] are not partisan.

q: If Cao Shuang had followed Huan Fan's advice, could the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs have been avoided?
reply:
Probably not. The sources do not show that Huan Fan's plan would have saved Cao Shuang. Cao Shuang's brothers hesitated over it, and by the time of the coup he had already given up most of his options.

The incident happened in 正始十年 (the 嘉平元年 of the 齊王紀 dating). Sima Yi memorialized against Cao Shuang and then occupied the Luo River bridge. Cao Shuang, cut off from the throne, was thrown into 「迫窘不知所爲」 ("pressed and not knowing what to do") [1]. Huan Fan, then Grand Minister of Agriculture, left the city and urged him to take the emperor to Xuchang and call in outside troops: 「範說爽使車駕幸許昌，招外兵」 (Huan Fan urged Cao Shuang to take the carriage to Xuchang and summon troops from outside) [1]. He also argued to Cao Xi that 「今卿與天子相隨，令於天下，誰敢不應者」 (with the emperor at your side and issuing orders to the realm, who would dare not to answer?) [1]. Cao Xi would not accept it, and the brothers 「猶豫未決」 (hesitated and did not decide) [1]. Huan Fan later pointed out that Cao Xi's camp was near the palace and that the Xuchang arsenal could supply weapons, but the concern was grain, and the seal of the Grain Office was in his own hands [8].

Sima Yi did not expect the plan to be carried out. He said, 「範畫策，爽必不能用範計」 (Huan Fan has made a plan, but Cao Shuang will certainly not use it) [1]. Jiang Ji said, in the 《晉書》 account, 「範則智矣，駑馬戀棧豆，爽必不能用也」 (Huan Fan is clever, but a worn-out horse loves the fodder in its stall; Cao Shuang will certainly not use it) [7]. These are opinions recorded in the sources, not evidence of what would have happened. What is recorded is that Sima Yi sent Xu Yun, Chen Tai and Jiang Ji with offers and a message, and the 《世語》 account says the palace officer Yin Damu swore on the Luo River that Cao Shuang would only be dismissed. Cao Shuang believed it and 「爽信之，罷兵」 (Cao Shuang believed it and withdrew his troops) [7]. He then sent men to admit guilt and ask for death: 「爽於是遣允、泰詣宣王，歸罪請死」 [1]. Huan Fan was later executed with the others and his family was exterminated [6].

The sources also show earlier points where Cao Shuang's position weakened. His advisers told him that Sima Yi's influence was too strong to leave to others, and Sima Yi then 「宣王遂稱疾避爽」 (feigned illness and kept away from Cao Shuang) [9]. Earlier, Dings Mi and Bi Gui had warned him: 「宣王有大志而甚得民心，不可以推誠委之」 (Sima Yi has great ambitions and wins the people's hearts; he cannot be trusted with real power) [5]. Cao Xi wrote a warning against extravagance, and Cao Shuang 「爽知其爲己發也，甚不恱」 (knew it was aimed at himself and was displeased) [9]. In the Luo Valley campaign of 正始五年, Yang Wei told him 「宜急還，不然將敗」 (he should turn back quickly or he would be defeated), and Cao Shuang withdrew [10]. Yang Zong also tried to stop him from giving up his seals and going out, saying 「公挾主握權，捨此以至東巿乎？」 (you hold the emperor and power; will you give this up and go to the East Market?) [11]. Huan Fan had also warned that the two brothers should not go out together: 「總萬機，典禁兵，不宜並出」 [18].

Chen Shou's judgment is that 「爽德薄位尊，沈溺盈溢，此固大易所著，道家所忌也」 (Cao Shuang had little virtue and high rank, and he indulged himself and overflowed; this is what the Great Changes records and what Daoists warn against) [21]. He also criticized Xiahou Xuan for never trying to correct Cao Shuang's faults: 「未聞匡弼其非」 [21].

My inference, based on these records, is that the decisive errors came before the crisis: keeping Sima Yi in a position he could resent, and the extravagance that gave him a reason to act. Huan Fan's plan was a real option at the moment of crisis, but it required a firm commitment that Cao Shuang and his brothers did not make. The sources do not allow us to test whether it would have worked. So the record supports the view that Cao Shuang's fall was very likely by the time of the coup, but not that Huan Fan's advice alone would have prevented it.
