q: What rank of strategist was Guo Jia, really, under Cao Cao?
reply:
Guo Jia's formal post under Cao Cao was 司空军祭酒, "Army Libationer of the Sikong's office." The records I checked never give him the title 军师祭酒, though the sources mention that office in general terms.

After Xun Yu recommended him, Cao Cao met him and said 「使孤成大業者，必此人也」, and the text then records that Cao Cao 「表為司空軍祭酒」 [2]. Cao Cao's memorial after Guo Jia's death calls him 「軍祭酒郭嘉，自從征伐，十有一年」 [1], and a memorial quoted in the commentary from 《魏書》 also calls him 「故軍祭酒郭嘉」 [3].

As a peerage, he was made 「封嘉洧陽亭侯」 [4]. His memorial recorded his posthumous honours: 「可增邑八百戶，並前千戶」 and the posthumous name 「諡曰貞侯」 [1].

The 祭酒 title was a staff advisory post. The records show several men holding it: Du Xi was 「丞相軍祭酒」 [11], Dong Zhao was 「轉拜司空軍祭酒」 [14], and Xu Gan was 「司空軍謀祭酒掾屬」 [12]. The records do not give a salary grade for Guo Jia's post. The 《武帝紀》 says that in 建安三年 Cao Cao 「初置軍師祭酒」 [8], but no record I found ties that title to Guo Jia.

His influence rested on his counsel rather than his title. Cao Cao's memorial says 「每有大議，臨敵制變。臣策未決，嘉輒成之。平定天下，謀功為高」 [1]. When Cao Cao asked how to deal with the Yuan brothers, Guo Jia advised turning south first, and Cao Cao said 「善」. The brothers then fought each other over Ji Province [4]. A passage quoted from 《傅子》 credits him with the plan to recruit well-known men from Qing, Ji, You and Bing provinces as 省事掾屬, saying 「皆嘉之謀也」 [7]. Chen Shou groups him with Cheng Yu, Dong Zhao, Liu Ye and Jiang Ji as 「世之奇士」 [17]. From these records, I infer that his importance to Cao Cao was greater than his title suggests, but the sources do not state this directly.

q: Should Xiahou Ba have defected to Shu Han?
reply:
**Short answer:** The records do not say whether he should have defected. They show why he fled, what happened to his family, and how Shu received him. Whether defection was the right choice depends on whether you weigh his personal safety or his loyalty to Wei more heavily. That is a judgment, not something the text settles.

**His reasons.** Xiahou Ba was a Wei general who had been "素爲曹爽所厚" (close to Cao Shuang) [2]. When Cao Shuang was executed, "聞爽誅，自疑，亡入蜀" (he heard of Cao Shuang's execution, grew suspicious of his own position, and fled into Shu) [2]. The Weilue, cited in Pei Songzhi's annotation, gives two further motives. First, Shu had killed his father Xiahou Yuan, so "霸常切齒，欲有報蜀意" (he had long gnashed his teeth and wanted revenge on Shu) [5]. Second, when Xiahou Xuan was recalled to the capital, "霸聞曹爽被誅而玄又徵，以爲祸必轉相及，心既内恐" (he feared the disaster would spread to him) [5]. The same source adds that he had quarrelled with Guo Huai, who replaced Xiahou Xuan as Western General, and this made him "尤不安" (even more uneasy) [5].

**What his fear was based on.** The purge was real. Xiahou Xuan was executed with his three clans, and "其餘親屬徙樂浪郡" (the remaining relatives were exiled to Lelang) [29]. Xiahou Ba's fear was therefore not baseless.

**What defection did for his family.** It did not spare them. His son was pardoned "以淵舊勳" (because of Xiahou Yuan's old merit), but was still "徙樂浪郡" (exiled to Lelang) [2]. Defection protected Xiahou Ba himself, but not his son.

**How Shu received him.** Shu welcomed him. Liu Chan told him, 「卿父自遇害於行間耳，非我先人之手刃也」 (your father was killed in battle, not by my predecessor's hand) [5]. The Weilue says Shu gave him "厚加爵寵" (generous rank and favour) [25]. Shu's own official record is brief: "右將軍夏侯霸來降" [8]. Pei's citation of the 《益部耆舊傳》 calls him "車騎將軍夏侯霸" [20]. But the same source shows that Zhang Yi, a Shu official, kept him at arm's length. When Xiahou Ba tried to confide in him, Zhang Yi replied, 「僕未知子，子未知我，大道在彼，何云託心乎！原三年之後徐陳斯言」 (I do not know you and you do not know me. The great road lies over there; how can we speak of confiding? Let us talk about this three years from now) [20].

**What the sources do not show.** The records do not say what Xiahou Ba did for Shu after he arrived, beyond his rank. They also do not give a verdict on his choice.

**The disputed prediction.** Pei cites two accounts of an exchange in which Xiahou Ba warned Jiang Wei about Zhong Hui. The 《世語》 version has Shu asking about Sima Yi's virtue, and Xiahou Ba answering 「自當作家門」 (he will attend to his own household) [1]. The 《漢晉春秋》 version has him say that Sima Yi is "未遑外事" (too busy to attend to foreign affairs) and that Zhong Hui would later be a threat, and adds 「後十五年而會果滅蜀」 (fifteen years later Zhong Hui did destroy Shu) [1]. Pei notes that this account "非出他書" (did not come from another book), so he suspects it was embellished [1]. This is Pei's own judgment, so the story should not be treated as firm evidence of Xiahou Ba's foresight.

**My inference.** The records support the view that his fear was real. Given the purge of Cao Shuang's circle and the exile of his relatives, fleeing was a reasonable response to a threat to his own life. But the sources do not show that defection was the wise or morally right course. It saved him and cost his son his home in Lelang. Shu gave him rank, but a Shu official held him at a distance. Whether he "should" have stayed with Wei depends on what you think a Wei general owed the Cao house, and the records do not decide that.

q: Chen Shou was born in Shu, so why does the Records of the Three Kingdoms contain so few accounts of Shu's deeds?
reply:
Your premise isn't confirmed by the sources I retrieved, which don't say where Chen Shou was born. They do show his ties to Shu. He wrote a local history of Yi province, 《益部耆舊傳》 [14], and his biography of 譙周 records that 譙周 was 「巴西西充國人也」 [8].

The most direct statement about why Shu's record is thin is Chen Shou's own evaluation of the Later Lord Liu Chan: 「又國不置史，注記無官，是以行事多遺，災異靡書。」 The state had no historiographer and no official keeping records, so events were often left out and disasters went unrecorded [34].

Chen Shou also excluded material he could not verify. In the Lu Kai biography, he says a memorial was 「虛實難明，故不著於篇」, but he still copied it out after the biography because it was a useful warning [9]. Applying that standard to Shu would shrink the Shu material. This is my inference from one example, not a statement he makes about Shu.

His Shu material also came partly from a specific commission. In the presentation memorial for Zhuge Liang's collected works, he says that Xun Xu and He Qiao had him 「使臣定故蜀丞相諸葛亮故事」 [17]. Much of his Shu material was therefore gathered for that purpose.

Some Shu judgments are vague rather than absent. Pei Songzhi objects that Chen Shou criticized Jiang Wan and Fei Yi 「今譏其未盡而不著其事，故使覽者不知所謂也」, meaning he did not say what the shortcomings were, so readers cannot tell what he meant [2].

Sun Sheng's 《異同記》 also quotes Chang Qu, a Shu historian, as saying that Chen Shou had once served under Zhuge Zhan and was 「為瞻所辱」, so he shifted blame onto Huang Hao [12]. This is a second-hand charge of personal bias, and the text does not let me verify it.

In short, the sources point to three things: Shu had no official historian, Chen Shou left out what he could not verify, and some of his Shu judgments are thin. These passages do not say how many Shu chapters there are compared with the other states, so I cannot make that comparison here.

q: Li Yan and Zhuge Liang were both regents named in Liu Bei's deathbed charge — so why was Zhuge Liang able to demote Li Yan to a commoner?
reply:
**Short answer:** Li Yan was not an equal co-regent. Liu Bei made Zhuge Liang the chief minister and Li Yan his deputy, and Zhuge controlled the administration. Li Yan was removed in the ninth year of the Jianxing reign after a dispute over supplies at Qishan. Li Yan blamed Zhuge for a withdrawal that Zhuge had ordered because the grain had stopped arriving, and Zhuge's memorial to the throne led to the demotion.

**Their positions.** Liu Bei's biography says that on his deathbed he 「託孤於丞相亮，尚書令李嚴為副」 (entrusted his heir to Chancellor Zhuge Liang, with Secretary-Director Li Yan as deputy) [5]. Li Yan's biography says the two of them 「並受遺詔輔少主」 (both received the will to assist the young ruler), but Li Yan was made 中都護 (Zhongdu Hu) and 「留鎮永安」 (left to garrison Yongan) [1]. Zhuge was Chancellor and 「錄尚書事」 (handled the Secretariat) [4]. After Liu Bei died, 「政事無巨細，咸決於亮」 (all government affairs, great or small, were decided by Zhuge) [8], and 「事無巨細，亮皆專之」 (he handled everything, great or small, himself) [23].

**The incident.** In the ninth year, Li Yan was in charge of pushing supply transport for Zhuge's Qishan campaign [12]. The record says 「值天霖雨，運糧不繼」 (rain fell for a long time and the grain could not keep up) [12]. Li Yan sent men to call Zhuge back, and Zhuge withdrew [12]. Li Yan then pretended surprise, saying 「軍糧饒足，何以便歸」 (the army has plenty of grain, why did it return?) [12]. He also told the throne that 「軍偽退，欲以誘賊與戰」 (the army was feigning retreat to lure the enemy into battle) [12]. Zhuge then produced his own letters and memorials showing the sequence of events, and Li Yan's contradictions were exposed. Li Yan 「辭窮情竭，首謝罪負」 (ran out of words and admitted his fault) [12].

**The demotion.** Zhuge's memorial said Li Yan, since the late emperor's death, had 「安身求名，無憂國之事」 (sought personal safety and reputation and did not concern himself with national affairs) [12]. It also said Li Yan had meant 「欲因行之際偪臣取利也」 (to use the campaign to press Zhuge for gain) [12]. Zhuge explained why he had kept Li Yan in high office: 「正以大事未定，漢室傾危，伐平之短，莫若褒之」 (because the great task was unfinished and the Han house was in danger, it was better to praise Li Yan than to expose his faults) [12]. The result was 「乃廢平為民，徙梓潼郡」 (Li Yan was stripped to commoner status and moved to Zitong) [12]. The Later Lord's annals date this to the eighth month of the ninth year: 「秋八月，都護李嚴廢徙梓潼郡」 [7]. A quoted memorial preserved in the commentary says that Zhuge and his senior officers jointly agreed to 「輒解平任，免官祿、節傳、印綬、符策，削其爵土」 (remove Li Yan's posts, salary, credentials, seals, and fief) [13]. So the decision was recorded as a joint resolution, not Zhuge's decree alone.

**Why Zhuge could do it.** The records do not describe a separate trial. Based on [4], [8], and [12], it appears that Zhuge's rank as Chancellor and his control of administration gave him the authority to bring the charge and have the removal entered on his memorial. The case also rested on Li Yan's conduct. A quoted memorial in the commentary says Li Yan 「受恩過量，不思忠報」 (received excessive favor and did not think of repaying it loyally) and 「迷罔上下」 (deceived both superiors and subordinates) [17]. Chen Shou's comment on several men, including Li Yan, says 「李嚴以幹局達」 (Li Yan rose through his ability) and 「招禍取咎，無不自己也」 (the calamities and blame all came from themselves) [16].

Li Yan died in the twelfth year, after hearing of Zhuge's death [12].

**Inference.** Zhuge's higher rank and his control of administration appear to be what allowed him to remove his co-regent. Li Yan's contradictory account of the withdrawal gave Zhuge the evidence to make the charge stick [12]. The records do not show whether the wording of Liu Bei's will limited Zhuge's authority in any way.

q: In the year Ma Su lost Chieh-t'ing, which year of which reign era was Shu-Han using? What year was it on the Wei side? And what year is that in the Western calendar?
reply:
Ma Su lost Jieting in the **sixth year of the Jianxing era (建興六年) of Shu-Han, which was 228 CE**. On the Wei side, that year was **the second year of the Taihe era (太和二年)**, also 228 CE.

- **Shu-Han:** Zhuge Liang had Ma Su command the front against Zhang He at Jieting: 「亮使馬謖督諸軍在前，與郃戰于街亭。謖違亮節度，舉動失宜，大為張郃所破」[1]. Ma Liang's biography dates this to Jianxing 6 with the line 「與魏將張郃戰於街亭，為郃所破」[5]. The Later Lord's annals also place the Shu campaign in Jianxing 6: 「六年春，亮出攻祁山，不克」[3].
- **Wei:** Guo Huai's biography dates the Shu advance and Ma Su's arrival at Jieting to the Taihe era: 「太和二年，蜀相諸葛亮出祁山，遣將軍馬謖至街亭」[14].
- **Western calendar:** The era conversion tool gives 建興六年 = 228 CE and 太和二年 = 228 CE.

q: Why did the Sun-Liu alliance keep quarreling over Jing Province, until Sun Quan finally stabbed Guan Yu in the back?
reply:
The record shows that the Jing dispute was a real conflict over territory, worsened by Guan Yu's pride and a refused marriage. It stayed on hold while Cao Cao was a threat. The sources do not use the phrase "stab in the back." They describe Sun's attack on Guan Yu as a planned surprise (襲), prepared in secret while relations were still formally peaceful.

The dispute began when Sun Quan asked for the Jing districts after Liu Bei took Yi Province. Liu Bei refused: 「吾方圖涼州，涼州定，乃盡以荊州與吳耳」 ("I am still trying to take Liangzhou; once Liangzhou is settled, I will hand all of Jing to Wu") [2]. Sun replied that this was a loan never returned: 「此假而不反，而欲以虛辭引歳」 ("This is borrowing without returning, and using empty words to stall for years") [2]. Sun then sent Lü Meng to take Changsha, Lingling and Guiyang, while Guan Yu drove out Sun's officials in the southern commanderies [2]. Liu Bei moved to Gongan and sent Guan Yu to Yiyang [3]. Only when Cao Cao entered Hanzhong did Liu Bei make peace, and the two sides split Jing: 「分荊州、江夏、長沙、桂陽東屬，南郡、零陵、武陵西屬」 [3]. That settlement was a truce forced by outside pressure, not a resolution.

Guan Yu's conduct made the situation worse. Sun had sent to ask for Guan Yu's daughter as a bride for his son, and Guan Yu 「罵辱其使，不許婚，權大怒」 ("insulted the envoy, refused the marriage, and Sun was furious") [14]. Guan Yu also looked down on the governors who served under him: 「素皆嫌羽輕己」 ("they had always resented Guan Yu for looking down on them") [14]. Chen Shou's judgment is that Guan Yu was 「剛而自矜」 ("unbending and self-regarding"), and that he 「以短取敗，理數之常也」 ("was defeated by his own weakness, as is the normal course of things") [27].

When Guan Yu attacked Cao Ren at Fan, Sun was 「內憚羽，外欲以爲己功」 ("inwardly afraid of Guan Yu, and outwardly wanting the credit for himself") and asked Cao Cao for permission to attack Guan Yu [13]. Sun had already been planning this: 「權時已與呂蒙陰議襲之，恐事洩」 ("Sun had already secretly discussed the attack with Lü Meng, and feared it would leak") [11]. Cao Cao's advisers argued that Sun could not be trusted: 「劉備、孫權，外親內疏，關羽得志，權必不原也」 ("Liu Bei and Sun Quan were close on the surface but distant inside; if Guan Yu gained his goal, Sun would certainly not accept it") [12]. Cao Cao followed this advice, and Sun 「引兵西襲公安、江陵」 ("led his troops west to surprise Gongan and Jiangling") [12]. Lü Meng 「先遣呂蒙襲公安」, and Mi Fang surrendered Jiangling, so Lü Meng took the city [13]. Guan Yu's army then collapsed: 「權已據江陵，盡虜羽士眾妻子，羽軍遂散」 ("Sun already held Jiangling and had captured the families of all of Guan Yu's soldiers, so his army scattered") [14]. Guan Yu was captured at Zhangxiang [13] and beheaded at Linju: 「斬羽及子平於臨沮」 ("beheaded Guan Yu and his son Ping at Linju") [14].

From these records, I infer that Sun's attack came from several things at once. The land dispute left Sun unwilling to accept Guan Yu's control of Jing. Guan Yu's refusal of the marriage and his contempt for his own subordinates made his position weaker. When Guan Yu was tied down at Fan and his rear was exposed, Sun saw a practical chance to take Jing by force. The records do not give Sun's own stated reasons, so this is an inference from the sequence of events, not a recorded motive. Sun's side was also not united on policy: Lu Su earlier argued for lending the territory to Liu Bei to settle the region, saying 「多操之敵，而自為樹黨，計之上也」 ("creating enemies for Cao Cao and building your own allies is the best plan") [4]. That shows the alliance was contested inside Wu as well as between Wu and Shu.

q: When Liu Pei marched south from Chia-meng against Liu Chang, he left Huo Chün to hold the city. How long did Liu Chang's forces besiege it? How many soldiers did Huo Chün have, and how was the siege finally broken?
reply:
Huo Chün's garrison held out against Liu Chang's forces for about a year. He had only several hundred men, and he broke the siege by sallying out with picked troops when the attackers grew careless. The text does not mention any relief force.

**The siege.** Huo Chün's biography says that when Liu Pei went back south from Jiameng to attack Liu Chang, he 「留峻守葭萌城」[1]. Liu Chang's generals then led more than ten thousand men up the Lang River against the city: 「後璋將扶禁、向存等帥萬餘人由閬水上，攻圍攻峻，且一年，不能下」[1]. The phrase 且一年 means "for about a year," and the attackers could not take the city.

**Huo Chün's troops.** The text gives the garrison as 「峻城中兵才數百人」[1], only several hundred soldiers.

**How the siege was broken.** The biography credits Huo Chün himself: 「伺其怠隙，選精銳出擊，大破之，即斬存首」[1]. He waited for a gap in the besiegers' vigilance, chose elite troops to sortie, routed them, and beheaded Xiang Cun on the spot.

**Afterward.** When Liu Pei took Shu, he 「乃分廣漢為梓潼郡，以峻為梓潼太守、裨將軍」[1], making Huo Chün Administrator of the new Zitong Commandery.

Do not confuse this with another long siege. When Liu Pei attacked Luocheng, the text says 「時璋子循守城，被攻且一年」[26], so Liu Chang's son, named 循 in the text, held that city under attack for about a year. That is a separate episode from the siege of Jiameng.

q: P'ang Te killed Kuo Yüan with his own hand in the battle at P'ing-yang. According to P'ei Sung-chih's commentary, how was Kuo Yüan related to Chung Yao? And how did Chung Yao react when he saw the head — what did he say?
reply:
Pei Songzhi's commentary, quoting the *Weilue* (《魏略》), says Guo Yuan was Zhong Yao's nephew. When Pang De later produced the head, Zhong Yao wept, and when Pang De apologized, Zhong Yao said Guo Yuan was a traitor to the state.

**Relationship:** The *Weilue* says 「援，鍾繇之甥」 ("Yuan was Zhong Yao's nephew") [2]. Zhong Yao's own biography describes Guo Yuan as the Hedong governor appointed by Yuan Shang, who came to Hedong with a large force [3].

**The killing:** Pang De's main biography says that as vanguard he attacked Guo Yuan and Gao Gan (高幹) at Pingyang and 「親斬援首」 ("personally beheaded Yuan") [1]. Ma Chao's biography repeats this: 「超將龐德親斬援首」 [10]. Zhong Yao's and Zhang Ji's biographies describe the victory as a joint attack by Zhong Yao and Ma Teng's forces, and they do not name Pang De as the man who took the head [3][13]. The sources differ on who gets the credit, and the main text of Pang De's biography is the one that names him.

**The head and Zhong Yao's reaction:** According to the *Weilue*, Pang De at first did not know whose head he had taken: 「德手斬一級，不知是援」 ("Pang De cut off one head by his own hand, not knowing it was Yuan's"). After the battle people said Guo Yuan had died but his head had not been found. Later Pang De produced a head from his quiver, and 「繇見之而哭」 ("Zhong Yao saw it and wept") [2]. When Pang De apologized, Zhong Yao replied: 「援雖我甥，乃國賊也。卿何謝之？」 ("Yuan, though he is my nephew, is a traitor to the state. Why do you apologize?") [2]

The quiver, the weeping and the exchange of words come only from the *Weilue* commentary. The main text records only that Pang De killed Guo Yuan.

q: Ts'ao Ts'ao asked P'ei Ch'ien about Liu Pei's abilities. How did P'ei Ch'ien assess him?
reply:
Pei Qian judged that Liu Bei could stir up trouble in the Central Plains but could not govern there. If Liu Bei seized an opening and held a strong position, Pei thought he could become the ruler of one region.

Cao Cao asked Pei, who had been in Jingzhou with Liu Bei, what he thought of Liu Bei's abilities. Pei answered: 「使居中國，能亂人而不能為治也。若乘閒守險，足以為一方主。」[1] In English: "Put him in the Central Plains, and he could throw people into disorder but could not bring order. If he took an opening and held a strong position, he would be enough to become the lord of one region."

This is Pei's own judgment, and the record does not say how Cao Cao responded. Earlier in the same biography, Pei had privately dismissed Liu Biao, saying 「劉牧非霸王之才，乃欲西伯自處，其敗無日矣」, roughly "Liu Biao lacks the talent of a hegemon and wants to play the Western Earl, so his defeat is not far off."[1]

q: When Liu Bei was gravely ill, Huang Yuan, the Grand Administrator of Hanjia, rebelled and burned Linqiong. How did Yang Hong work out where Huang Yuan would go, and how was he captured?
reply:
Yang Hong judged that Huang Yuan would flee down the river toward Wu, and he posted guards at the Nan'an gorge on that route. Two generals then took Huang alive.

Huang Yuan, Grand Administrator of Hanjia, had long been disliked by Zhuge Liang. When he heard Liu Bei was gravely ill, he feared future trouble, rebelled with his whole commandery, and burned Linqiong. Zhuge Liang had gone east to check on the ruler's illness, and Chengdu was nearly empty, so Huang felt even less restrained: 「時亮東行省疾，成都單虛，是以元益無所憚」 ("At that time Liang had gone east to visit the ill ruler, Chengdu was nearly empty, and so Yuan was even less restrained") [1].

Those present proposed that if Huang could not besiege Chengdu, he would go through Yuexi and seize Nanzhong. Yang Hong disagreed, judging from Huang's character: 「元素信凶暴，無他恩信，何能辦此？」 ("Yuan has always been violent and has no benevolence or trust to speak of; how could he manage that?") [1]. He then described two courses for Huang: 「不過乘水東下，冀主上平安，面縛歸死；如其有異，奔吳求活耳」 ("He would only go down the river eastward, hoping the ruler was safe, and surrender bound; if something had happened, he would flee to Wu to save himself") [1].

By this reasoning, Yang's conclusion was that Huang would take the river route east, which was the one to watch. This is an inference from his assessment of Huang's character and the two options. The record does not say how he weighed the other possibilities.

Yang Hong first reported to the crown prince, then had the prince's personal guards sent out under generals Chen Hu (陳曶) and Zheng Chuo (鄭綽). He told them: 「敕曶、綽但於南安峽口遮即便得矣」 ("Order Hu and Chuo simply to block the mouth of the Nan'an gorge, and they will capture him right there") [1]. The text then says that Chen and Zheng 「承洪言，果生獲元」 ("followed Yang's words and did indeed capture Yuan alive") [1]. The record gives no further details of the fighting or of Huang's fate.

For his service, Yang Hong was granted the rank of Guannei Marquis (關內侯) in the first year of the Jianxing era and was again made Grand Administrator of Shu Commandery [1]. Earlier, Li Yan had recommended him, and when Zhuge Liang asked him whether to send troops to Hanzhong, he advised that they should [11].

q: Which painter, while painting a screen for Sun Quan, let a drop of ink fall on the silk by mistake and turned it into a fly — so lifelike that Sun Quan took it for a real fly and raised his hand to flick it away?
reply:
The painter was **Cao Buxing** (曹不兴). The account comes from Pei Songzhi's commentary, which quotes the *Wu Lu* (《吴录》), and not from Chen Shou's main text.

The commentary reads: 「曹不興善畫，權使畫屏風，誤落筆點素，因就以作蠅。既進御，權以爲生蠅，舉手彈之。」[1] In English: Cao Buxing was skilled at painting. Sun Quan had him paint a screen. He accidentally let his brush drop a spot onto the silk, and he then made it into a fly. When it was presented to Sun Quan, Sun Quan took it for a live fly and raised his hand to flick it away.

The same passage says that Cao Buxing was one of eight men of the period admired for their skills, known as 「八絕」, along with Wu Fan, Liu Dun, and Zhao Da.[1] Because the story appears only in this commentary, it should be read as a later anecdote recorded by Pei Songzhi rather than as part of the official history.

q: How did Cao Pi's Empress Zhen die? Do the historical sources disagree about it?
reply:
**Short answer:** The sources disagree. Chen Shou's main text says Cao Pi (Emperor Wen of Wei) ordered Empress Zhen to die in the sixth month of the second year of the Huangchu era. A *Wei Shu* account quoted in Pei Songzhi's notes says she fell ill and died. Pei doubts that account and points to a forced death. None of the sources describes how the order was carried out.

**The main text:** Zhen was favored early on. After Cao Pi took the throne, the Shanyang Gong's daughters entered the palace, and Lady Guo and Consorts Li and Yin were favored. The text says: 「后愈失意，有怨言。帝大怒，二年六月，遣使賜死，葬於鄴。」[12] ("She grew more and more unhappy and voiced complaints. The emperor was furious, and in the sixth month of the second year he sent an envoy to order her death. She was buried at Ye.") 「賜死」 means she was ordered to die. It does not say whether she took her own life or was killed.

**The *Wei Shu* account:** Pei quotes the *Wei Shu* as saying that Cao Pi sent a seal letter to bring Zhen to court as empress. She declined, citing illness. 「會后疾遂篤，夏六月丁卯，崩於鄴」[6] ("Her illness grew worse, and in the sixth month, on the day dingmao, she died at Ye"). Cao Pi then mourned her and conferred an empress's seal posthumously.

**Pei Songzhi's rejection:** Pei writes that under the Spring and Autumn principle, a ruler's great wrongs were concealed and minor ones were not recorded. He concludes: 「文帝之不立甄氏，及加殺害，事有明審」[6] ("Wen's failure to establish Zhen as empress, and his having her killed, are clearly documented"). He therefore doubts the *Wei Shu*'s praise of her virtues and approves Chen Shou's removal of such material. This is Pei's own judgment, not the *Wei Shu*'s.

**Other sources:**
- The annals of Emperor Wen record only: 「丁卯，夫人甄氏卒」[13] ("On dingmao, Lady Zhen died"). They give no cause, and the date matches the *Wei Shu* account.
- The *Weilüe*, quoted in Pei's notes, says Emperor Ming grieved over Zhen's death. When Lady Guo's own funeral was held, it followed "Zhen's precedent," with the hair covering the face [19]. It also refers to 「見譖之禍」 ("the disaster of being slandered") [19].
- The *Han-Jin Chunqiu*, quoted in the same note, says 「甄后之誅，由郭后之寵也」 ("Zhen's execution came from Lady Guo's favor"). It adds that at Zhen's burial her hair was loosened over her face and her mouth was stuffed with chaff. Later, when Emperor Ming learned of this, he forced Lady Guo to die [19]. This source calls Zhen's death an execution (誅), while the main text says only 「賜死」.
- The Guo Empress biography says 「甄后之死，由后之寵也」 ("Zhen's death came from Lady Guo's favor") [20].

**My inference:** The main text, Pei's comment, the *Weilüe* and the *Han-Jin Chunqiu* all point to a death that Cao Pi forced or caused through his displeasure. The illness account appears only in the *Wei Shu* text Pei quotes, and Pei rejects it. The annals' bare 「卒」 fits either version, so it does not settle the question. From Pei's criticism, I infer that the illness story was the official version, but the sources do not prove this. They also do not give the method of death, and I found no account that states it.

q: Which Cavalier Regular Palace Attendant of Wu got drunk and collapsed at the banquet Sun Hao held for Ding Zhong on his return from an embassy to Jin, and was beheaded in the hall on Sun Hao's orders? In which year?
reply:
The man was **Wang Fan (王蕃)**, and the year was **266 CE** (Sun Hao's Ganlu 2).

The main biography of Wang Fan records: 「甘露二年，丁忠使晉還，皓大會群臣，蕃沉醉頓伏。」[1] ("In the second year of Ganlu, Ding Zhong returned from his mission to Jin, and Sun Hao held a great assembly of his officials. Fan became drunk and collapsed.") Sun Hao was displeased and had Fan carried out. When Fan asked to return to the banquet, he was still drunk. Sun Hao then became furious and ordered him beheaded: 「皓大怒，呵左右於殿下斬之」[1] ("Sun Hao was furious, and shouted for his attendants to behead him below the hall"). The generals Teng Mu and Liu Ping pleaded for Fan, but could not save him. Ding Zhong's mission had been earlier: Sun Hao sent him, with Zhang Yan, to condole Jin's Emperor Wen in the first year of Baoding. [4]

The *Jiangbiao zhuan* (江表傳), quoted by Pei Songzhi, gives a different account of the killing. It says Sun Hao asked Fan the meaning of an archery saying, and that Fan was killed 「即於殿上斩蕃」 ("right in the hall") before the head was mutilated afterward. It notes that this differs from the main text. [5] It does not give a year, so the date of 266 rests on the main text.

Pei Songzhi also notes a dating problem in the *Wu lu* (吳錄). That work tells a different story about Fan mocking Wan Yu, and Pei points out that Ding Zhong's return was in the spring of that year, while Wan Yu only became chancellor later in the autumn. Pei says the *Wu lu* account conflicts with the main text on this point. [5]

q: Who had the courtesy name Wenze?
reply:
Two men in the *Sanguozhi* had the courtesy name Wenze (文则): Yu Jin (于禁) of Wei and Wu Fan (吴范) of Wu.

**Yu Jin** is recorded as「于禁字文則，泰山鉅平人也」[1] (Yu Jin, courtesy name Wenze, was from Juping in Taishan). He served Cao Cao, and Chen Shou groups him with Zhang Liao, Le Jin, Zhang He and Xu Huang as famous generals of the time [6]. In the 24th year of the Jian'an era he was sent to aid Cao Ren against Guan Yu, and when floodwaters swept his army, he surrendered; the text says he was later in Wu, and Sun Quan returned him to Wei after Wei's Emperor Wen took the throne [2]. Chen Shou's evaluation says「最號毅重，然弗克其終」[8] (he was known for steadfast gravity but did not end well).

**Wu Fan** is recorded as「吳範字文則，會稽上虞人也」[9] (Wu Fan, courtesy name Wenze, was from Shangyu in Kuaiji). He was known for calendrical calculation and reading omens, and Sun Quan made him Grand Astrologer (領太史令) [13]. He died in the 5th year of the Huangwu era [16].

q: How did Xu Zhu realize that Xu Ta and the others were plotting to assassinate Cao Cao? And how did he deal with them?
reply:
Xu Zhu (许褚) noticed the plot when his own unease sent him back to his post, and he killed the plotters as soon as he saw their faces change. The source does not name Cao Cao as the target. It says only that the men "plotted rebellion," but Xu Zhu's role as guard makes that the likely target, which is my inference.

The plotters were 徐他 (Xu Ta) and others among Xu Zhu's usual attendants. Because Xu Zhu was always at the ruler's side, they feared him and waited for a day when he was off duty: 「時常從士徐他等謀為逆，以褚常侍左右，憚之不敢發。伺褚休下日，他等懷刀入。」[1] ("Xu Ta and others among his usual attendants plotted rebellion. Because Xu Zhu was always beside the ruler, they feared him and did not dare to act. They waited for a day when Xu Zhu was off duty, and then they entered carrying knives.")

Xu Zhu first realized something was wrong on his way to his lodging, when his heart was disturbed and he turned back to his post: 「褚至下捨心動，即還侍。」[1] ("Xu Zhu reached his lodging and his heart was disturbed, so he immediately returned to attend the ruler.") The plotters did not know he had come back. They entered the tent, saw him, and were astonished. 「他等不知，入帳見褚，大驚愕。他色變，褚覺之，即擊殺他等。」[1] ("The others did not know, so they entered the tent and saw Xu Zhu, and they were greatly astonished. Xu Ta's face changed, Xu Zhu perceived it, and he immediately struck down the group.")

So he dealt with them by killing them on the spot. Cao Cao then trusted him even more and kept him constantly at his side: 「太祖益親信之，出入同行，不離左右。」[1] ("The Grand Ancestor trusted him even more, and he went in and out together with him and never left his side.")

Pei Songzhi's own comment, which is not part of the original text, notes that when Xu Ta plotted rebellion Xu Zhu's heart was moved, and it ranks his loyalty alongside that of Jin Midi: 「徐佗謀逆而許褚心動，忠誠之至遠同於日磾」[5] ("Xu Ta plotted rebellion and Xu Zhu's heart was moved; his loyalty reached the utmost, equal to that of Jin Midi."). Note that the spelling 徐佗 there is the same person as 徐他.

q: What did Liu Bei say to Zhuge Liang when he entrusted his heir to him on his deathbed? How did Zhuge Liang reply? And what instructions did Liu Bei leave for the Later Sovereign?
reply:
In spring 223 CE, while Liu Bei was gravely ill at Yong'an, he summoned Zhuge Liang and told him that if his heir could be supported, Zhuge should support him, and if not, Zhuge could take power himself. Zhuge Liang wept and pledged his loyalty to death. In a separate edict to his son Liu Shan, Liu Bei told him to serve Zhuge Liang as he would a father.

The words to Zhuge Liang are recorded in his biography. Liu Bei said: 「君才十倍曹丕，必能安國，終定大事。若嗣子可輔，輔之；如其不才，君可自取。」[13] ("Your talent is ten times that of Cao Pi; you will surely secure the state and complete the great task. If my heir can be assisted, assist him; if he is unworthy, you may take the position yourself.") Zhuge Liang answered in tears: 「臣敢竭股肱之力，效忠貞之節，繼之以死！」[13] ("Your minister dares to exhaust the strength of his arms and legs, render the loyalty of a faithful servant, and follow it with death!") The date 章武三年 corresponds to 223 CE.

The instruction to the heir came in an edict issued alongside those words: 「汝與丞相從事，事之如父。」[13] ("You and the Chancellor shall work together; serve him as you would a father.") Liu Shan succeeded in the fifth month, 「時年十七」[16] (aged seventeen).

Liu Bei's will also set mourning rules. Zhuge Liang's memorial to the Later Sovereign reports that the officials were to 「發哀，滿三日除服，到葬期復如禮」[14] (mourn, remove mourning clothes after three days, and observe the rites again at burial). These provisions concern the officials' mourning, not Liu Shan's own conduct.

Sun Sheng's comment, quoted in Pei Songzhi's annotation, criticized the remark about Zhuge Liang taking power. He wrote: 「苟所寄忠賢，則不須若斯之誨，如非其人，不宜啟篡逆之塗」[9] (if the person entrusted is loyal and worthy, such instruction is unnecessary; if he is not the right person, it should not open the way to usurpation). He also said that the outcome was fortunate only because 「幸值劉禪闇弱，無猜險之性」[9] (Liu Shan happened to be weak and without a suspicious or treacherous nature). Sun Sheng rejected the view, held by some, that Liu Bei meant to strengthen Zhuge Liang's trust and unify the people of Shu [9].

Chen Shou's evaluation of Liu Bei praises him for 「及其舉國託孤於諸葛亮，而心神無貳，誠君臣之至公」[17] (when he entrusted the state to Zhuge Liang without any second thought, it was a true example of fairness between ruler and minister). This is Chen Shou's judgment, not a record of events.

q: How many different people named Zhao Da appear in the Records of the Three Kingdoms, and what did each of them do?
reply:
The *Records of the Three Kingdoms* contain **two** people named Zhao Da (赵达), and possibly a third if the two Wei passages describe different men. The lookup lists three entries, but the two Wei entries describe the same kind of official under Cao Cao, so they probably refer to one man. Neither passage gives his given name, so this is not certain.

**1. Zhao Da the diviner (吴书, 吴范刘惇赵达传).** He was from Henan and studied the "Nine Palaces, One Calculation" (九宫一算) method. He believed the southeast held royal energy, so 「謂東南有王者氣，可以避難，故脫身渡江」[4]. He crossed the Yangzi to escape the north. Sun Quan used his forecasts: 「每令達有所推步，皆如其言」, but Zhao Da never revealed his method, and 「由此見薄，祿位不至」[12]. Asked how long Sun Quan's reign would last, he answered 「高祖建元十二年，陛下倍之」[14], a remark recorded in Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting 《吳書》. Pei Songzhi's annotation quoting Gan Bao's 《晉紀》 also records his prediction that Wu would decline: 「吳衰庚子歳」[16]. He died when he had calculated: 「後如期死」[12].

**2. Zhao Da the Wei 校事 (secret-service officer).**
- In Gao Rou's biography, 「時置校事盧洪、趙達等，使察羣下」[1]. Gao Rou objected. Cao Cao later 「達等後姧利發，太祖殺之以謝於柔」[1], so he had Zhao Da and his colleagues executed to answer Gao Rou's complaint.
- In Xu Miao's biography, 「校事趙達問以曹事，邈曰：『中聖人。』達白之太祖，太祖甚怒」[18]. Xu Miao had been drinking during a ban on alcohol, and 「中聖人」 was his evasive answer. Xianyu Fu spoke for him, and he 「竟坐得免刑」[18].

Both Wei passages show a 校事 under Cao Cao, which suggests they describe the same man. The text does not say so. It also does not say whether the Xu Miao episode came before or after the execution in Gao Rou's biography.

The diviner and the Wei official are almost certainly different men. The diviner served Sun Quan in Wu and died at home as he had calculated. The 校事 served Cao Cao in the north and was executed. The records do not say they were related, so this is an inference from their different careers and fates.
